question: VMs in prod-vpc must resolve hosts under onprem.example.com. The authoritative DNS servers for that domain run on premises at 192.168.10.53 and 192.168.10.54, reachable over HA VPN. What should you configure in Cloud DNS?
options: A DNS server policy on prod-vpc with inbound forwarding enabled for the on-premises servers
A public zone for onprem.example.com with copies of the on-premises A records added manually
A DNS peering zone for onprem.example.com that points at the on-premises network's resolvers
A private forwarding zone for onprem.example.com that targets the two on-premises DNS servers
explanation: A private forwarding zone sends queries for the domain from authorized VPC networks to the on-premises name servers over hybrid connectivity. An inbound server policy solves the reverse case, letting on-premises clients resolve Cloud DNS names. A public zone exposes manually copied records that drift, and DNS peering zones point to another VPC network, not to on-premises servers.

question: A web application behind a global external Application Load Balancer is receiving SQL injection and cross-site scripting attempts. You want to filter these requests before they reach the backend VMs. What should you do?
options: Attach a Cloud Armor security policy with preconfigured WAF rules to the load balancer's backend service
Add a VPC firewall rule that denies TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 to the backend VMs at a priority of 100
Create a Private Service Connect endpoint in front of the load balancer to hide the backend addresses
Configure Cloud NAT on the backend subnet so that responses use addresses that attackers cannot reach
explanation: Cloud Armor security policies attach to backend services of external Application Load Balancers and include preconfigured WAF rules for attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting. A layer 3 and 4 deny rule cannot inspect request content and would block all users. Private Service Connect and Cloud NAT do not inspect or filter HTTP requests.

question: Before changing production, an engineer wants to see exactly which Google Cloud resources a Terraform configuration would create, change or destroy, without modifying anything. Which command should they run?
options: terraform validate
terraform plan
terraform apply -auto-approve
terraform init -upgrade
explanation: terraform plan compares the configuration with the state and real infrastructure and shows the proposed changes without applying them. terraform validate only checks syntax and internal consistency, terraform apply -auto-approve makes the changes without a prompt, and terraform init installs providers and configures the backend.

question: A developer clones a repository whose Terraform configuration uses the hashicorp/google provider and a gcs backend. Running terraform plan immediately fails, reporting that the backend and providers have not been initialized. What should they run first?
options: terraform apply -refresh-only, to download providers and read the remote state
terraform init, to configure the backend and download the required providers
terraform fmt -recursive, to normalize files so the providers can be detected
gcloud components install terraform, to add the google provider to the CLI
explanation: terraform init initializes a working directory: it configures the backend and installs the providers the configuration requires, and it must run before plan or apply. Refresh-only apply still needs an initialized directory, fmt only reformats files, and the provider is not installed through gcloud components.

question: Five engineers run Terraform against the same Google Cloud project. They keep overwriting each other's local terraform.tfstate files. They need shared state that supports locking. What should they do?
options: Configure a gcs backend that stores the state in a Cloud Storage bucket, ideally with versioning enabled
Commit terraform.tfstate to the Git repository and require pull requests before each terraform apply
Copy terraform.tfstate to a Cloud Storage bucket with gcloud storage cp after every successful apply
Keep the state in each engineer's Cloud Shell home directory and synchronize it with gcloud storage rsync
explanation: The gcs backend stores Terraform state in a Cloud Storage bucket and supports state locking, so concurrent runs cannot corrupt it, and bucket versioning helps recover earlier state. Committing state to Git or copying it manually offers no locking and risks stale or conflicting state, and per-user copies do not create a single source of truth.

question: A Cloud Storage bucket was created manually in the console. The team has now written a matching google_storage_bucket resource in Terraform and wants Terraform to manage the existing bucket without recreating it. What should they do?
options: Run terraform apply, which detects the manually created bucket and records it in the state automatically
Run terraform apply -refresh-only, which adds any matching resources it finds in the project to the state
Mark the resource with terraform taint so that the next apply adopts the existing bucket instead of creating one
Import the existing bucket into Terraform state with terraform import or an import block, then run terraform plan
explanation: Importing records the existing bucket in state under the configured resource address, and a following plan shows any differences to fix. A normal apply would try to create a bucket with the same name and fail. A refresh-only apply only updates resources already tracked in state, and taint forces replacement of tracked resources rather than adopting new ones.

question: A Terraform configuration must set an argument on a Google Cloud resource that is only available in a beta API. The rest of the configuration uses the generally available google provider. What is the standard approach?
options: Set version = "beta" in the required_providers block so the google provider switches to the beta API
Call gcloud beta commands from a local-exec provisioner after Terraform creates the resource normally
Declare the google-beta provider and set provider = google-beta on the resource that needs the beta argument
Deploy through Infrastructure Manager, which automatically runs every configuration against the beta API
explanation: Google publishes two Terraform providers, google and google-beta, and individual resources can use the beta provider through the provider meta-argument. A version constraint selects a provider release, not an API track. Shelling out to gcloud bypasses Terraform state, and Infrastructure Manager runs the configuration as written.

question: Your Terraform for core networking lives in the network directory on the main branch of https://github.com/acme/infra.git. You want Google Cloud to run Terraform and keep the state, using the service account im-sa, without running Terraform yourself. Which command creates and applies the deployment?
options: gcloud infra-manager deployments apply projects/acme-prod/locations/us-central1/deployments/net-core --service-account=projects/acme-prod/serviceAccounts/im-sa@acme-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com --git-source-repo=https://github.com/acme/infra.git --git-source-directory=network --git-source-ref=main

gcloud infra-manager previews create net-core --location=us-central1 --service-account=projects/acme-prod/serviceAccounts/im-sa@acme-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com --git-source-repo=https://github.com/acme/infra.git --git-source-directory=network --git-source-ref=main
gcloud deployment-manager deployments create net-core --template=https://github.com/acme/infra.git/network/main.tf --project=acme-prod --automatic-rollback-on-error

gcloud builds submit https://github.com/acme/infra.git --git-source-dir=network --git-source-revision=main --region=us-central1 --service-account=projects/acme-prod/serviceAccounts/im-sa@acme-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com
explanation: gcloud infra-manager deployments apply creates or updates an Infrastructure Manager deployment, which runs Terraform in Cloud Build and stores the state for each revision; Git sources use the git-source flags. A preview only shows proposed changes. Deployment Manager does not run Terraform and its support ended in 2026, and a plain Cloud Build submission leaves you to script Terraform and manage state yourself.

question: A team still deploys infrastructure with Deployment Manager templates. Leadership wants a Google-managed service that runs Terraform for them, keeps the state and revision history, and needs no self-managed CI runners. Which service should they adopt?
options: Deployment Manager with Jinja
Helm with a values file
Infrastructure Manager
Fabric FAST stage outputs
explanation: Infrastructure Manager is Google Cloud's managed service for deploying Terraform configurations; it runs Terraform in Cloud Build and stores state and revisions. Deployment Manager is the product being replaced and lost support on April 1, 2026. Helm packages Kubernetes applications, and Fabric FAST is a set of Terraform landing-zone blueprints, not a Terraform runner.

question: Config Connector is installed on a GKE cluster, and a namespace is configured to manage resources in project acme-dev. A developer has written bucket.yaml with apiVersion storage.cnrm.cloud.google.com/v1beta1 and kind StorageBucket. How do they create the bucket?
options: Run gcloud storage buckets create --from-file=bucket.yaml --project=acme-dev from Cloud Shell
Run kubectl apply -f bucket.yaml in that namespace and let Config Connector create the bucket
Run helm install bucket ./bucket.yaml --namespace=acme-dev to render and apply the manifest
Run terraform apply -var-file=bucket.yaml so the Kubernetes manifest becomes Terraform input
explanation: Config Connector represents Google Cloud resources as Kubernetes custom resources, so applying the manifest with kubectl creates the object and the controller creates and reconciles the actual bucket. gcloud storage does not read Kubernetes manifests, Helm installs charts rather than single resource files, and Terraform does not take Kubernetes manifests as variable files.

question: You packaged a Helm chart as web-0.3.0.tgz and want to store it in Artifact Registry in us-west1 for project acme-prod so clusters can install it. Which steps are correct?
options: Create a repository with --repository-format=helm, then run helm push web-0.3.0.tgz https://us-west1-helm.pkg.dev/acme-prod/charts
Create a repository with --repository-format=docker, then run docker push us-west1-docker.pkg.dev/acme-prod/charts/web-0.3.0.tgz
Create a Cloud Storage bucket with gcloud storage buckets create gs://acme-charts, then run helm push web-0.3.0.tgz gs://acme-charts
Create a repository with --repository-format=docker, then run helm push web-0.3.0.tgz oci://us-west1-docker.pkg.dev/acme-prod/charts
explanation: Artifact Registry stores Helm charts as OCI artifacts in Docker-format repositories, and helm push uploads a packaged chart to an oci:// URL for that repository. helm push needs an oci:// registry reference rather than an https:// or gs:// URL, and docker push expects container images rather than packaged chart archives.

question: The Helm release storefront on a GKE cluster was upgraded to revision 5, and the new version is failing. Revision 4 was healthy. Which command returns the release to revision 4?
options: helm upgrade storefront --revision=4
kubectl rollout undo storefront --to-revision=4
helm rollback storefront 4
helm uninstall storefront --keep-history=4
explanation: helm rollback takes the release name and the revision to restore, and records the result as a new revision. helm upgrade has no option to target an earlier revision, kubectl rollout undo acts on individual Deployments rather than a Helm release, and helm uninstall removes the release.

question: A large enterprise is starting on Google Cloud. It wants an opinionated, production-ready Terraform reference implementation for its landing zone, built in stages that handle organization setup, the resource hierarchy, shared networking, security and a project factory. What should it use?
options: Application Design Center templates
Config Connector resource manifests
Deployment Manager organization templates
Cloud Foundation Fabric FAST
explanation: Fabric FAST is Google's Terraform-based blueprint for designing and building an organization's landing zone in stages that pass outputs to later stages. Application Design Center focuses on application architectures, Config Connector manages individual resources from Kubernetes, and Deployment Manager is no longer supported.

question: An operator is in the Google Cloud console investigating a spike in errors on a Cloud Run service. They want an AI assistant in the console that can explore related logs, metrics and alerts in natural language and run an AI-driven investigation into the root cause. Which tool fits?
options: Gemini Cloud Assist
Gemini CLI
Google Antigravity
Application Design Center
explanation: Gemini Cloud Assist is the AI assistant in the Google Cloud console that helps operate and troubleshoot resources, including AI-driven Investigations. Gemini CLI is a terminal agent, Google Antigravity is an agentic development environment for writing software, and Application Design Center is for designing and deploying application architectures.

question: A developer wants a desktop development environment where AI agents plan and carry out coding tasks across an editor, a terminal and a browser, work asynchronously from a manager view, and produce artifacts such as task lists and screenshots to verify their work. Which tool should they use?
options: Gemini Cloud Assist
Google Antigravity
Cloud Asset Inventory
Application Design Center
explanation: Google Antigravity is an agentic development platform with an AI-powered editor and a manager surface where agents plan, execute and verify tasks across the editor, terminal and browser, producing artifacts for review. Gemini Cloud Assist works inside the Google Cloud console, Cloud Asset Inventory lists resources, and Application Design Center designs cloud application architectures.

question: Your team is comparing AI-assisted tools named in the ACE exam guide. Which pairing of tool and task is accurate?
options: Gemini CLI: an open-source terminal agent that uses a reason-and-act loop with built-in tools and MCP servers
Application Design Center: an open-source terminal agent that edits local Terraform files from Cloud Shell
Gemini Cloud Assist: a desktop IDE in which several coding agents test front-end features in a browser
Google Antigravity: a console panel that runs AI investigations when a Cloud Monitoring alert fires
explanation: Gemini CLI is an open-source AI agent for the terminal that uses a reason-and-act loop with its built-in tools and local or remote MCP servers. The other pairings swap capabilities: the terminal agent is Gemini CLI, the agentic desktop IDE is Antigravity, and console-based alert investigations belong to Gemini Cloud Assist.

question: In Application Design Center, a platform team built approved application templates in its own space. Development teams that work in other spaces must be able to find and use these templates. What should the platform team do?
options: Export the templates as Helm charts and push them to a shared Artifact Registry repository
Give the development teams edit access to the platform team's application drafts instead
Share a catalog that contains the approved templates with the development teams' spaces
Convert each template into a Fabric FAST stage so other spaces can import its outputs
explanation: In Application Design Center, catalogs are the repositories that hold approved templates, and a space can receive catalogs shared from other spaces, so developers can build application drafts from them. Helm charts and Fabric FAST stages are separate tools, and sharing drafts does not publish governed templates.

question: A Windows Server VM named win-app-1 in us-east1-b has no external IP address. A firewall rule already allows TCP 3389 from 35.235.240.0/20, and you hold the IAP-secured Tunnel User role. You want to open an RDP session from your laptop by pointing your RDP client at localhost:3390. Which command should you run first?
options: gcloud compute ssh win-app-1 --tunnel-through-iap --zone=us-east1-b -- -L 3390:localhost:3389
gcloud compute instances add-access-config win-app-1 --zone=us-east1-b, then connect to port 3389
gcloud compute connect-to-serial-port win-app-1 --port=3389 --zone=us-east1-b --extra-args=local=3390
gcloud compute start-iap-tunnel win-app-1 3389 --local-host-port=localhost:3390 --zone=us-east1-b
explanation: gcloud compute start-iap-tunnel opens an IAP TCP forwarding tunnel from a local port to a port on the VM, which is how you reach RDP on a VM without an external IP. The ssh option relies on an SSH server, which a default Windows VM does not run. Adding an access config gives the VM a public IP, which defeats the purpose, and the serial port command connects to the virtual serial console, not to RDP.

question: Your project has the metadata key enable-oslogin set to TRUE. A database administrator was granted the Compute OS Login role (roles/compute.osLogin) and can SSH into the VMs, but every sudo command fails. The administrator needs root-level access on these VMs. What should you do?
options: Add the administrator's public SSH key to the project metadata so that the key gains sudo rights on each VM.
Grant the administrator the Compute Instance Admin (v1) role so that sudo is allowed inside the guest OS.
Set enable-oslogin to FALSE on the VMs so that the administrator's existing account is placed in the sudoers group.
Grant the administrator the Compute OS Admin Login role (roles/compute.osAdminLogin) instead of the OS Login role.
explanation: With OS Login, roles/compute.osLogin grants a standard login and roles/compute.osAdminLogin grants login with administrator (sudo) rights. Metadata-based SSH keys are ignored while OS Login is enabled. Compute Instance Admin manages VM resources but does not give OS Login sudo rights, and turning off OS Login abandons centralized IAM-based access.

question: An auditor asks for a list of only the Compute Engine VMs that are currently running in your project, across all zones, showing each VM's name and zone. Which command returns this?
options: gcloud compute instances describe --all --filter="status=RUNNING" --format="table(name,zone)"
gcloud compute instances list --zones=all --status=RUNNING --format="table(name,zone)"
gcloud compute instance-groups list-instances --filter="status=RUNNING" --format="table(name,zone)"
gcloud compute instances list --filter="status=RUNNING" --format="table(name,zone)"
explanation: gcloud compute instances list returns VMs in every zone by default, and the --filter flag narrows the result to those whose status is RUNNING. The describe command takes a single instance name and has no --all option. There is no --status flag on instances list, and list-instances only shows members of a single instance group.

question: The snapshot schedule daily-14d is attached to the disk orders-data in us-central1-a. You created a replacement schedule and now try to delete daily-14d with gcloud compute resource-policies delete, but the request fails because the schedule is still in use. What should you do?
options: Run gcloud compute resource-policies delete daily-14d --region=us-central1 --force to detach it from all disks and delete it.
Run gcloud compute snapshots delete for every snapshot created by daily-14d so nothing depends on it, then delete the schedule.
Run gcloud compute disks remove-resource-policies orders-data --resource-policies=daily-14d --zone=us-central1-a, then delete the schedule.
Run gcloud compute disks update orders-data --clear-resource-policies --zone=us-central1-a, then delete the schedule.
explanation: You cannot delete a snapshot schedule that is attached to a disk; you must first detach it with gcloud compute disks remove-resource-policies. The delete command has no --force option that detaches disks. Deleting the existing snapshots does not detach the schedule, and disks update has no --clear-resource-policies flag. Snapshots already created by the schedule are kept after the schedule is deleted.

question: A snapshot schedule backs up many short-lived disks. When a disk is deleted, its automatically created snapshots currently stay forever and storage costs keep rising. You want auto snapshots of deleted disks to keep expiring under the schedule's retention window. Which setting should the new schedule use?
options: --on-source-disk-delete=keep-auto-snapshots
--on-source-disk-delete=apply-retention-policy
--max-retention-days=0 with --guest-flush enabled
--storage-location set to a regional bucket location
explanation: The on-source-disk-delete setting controls what happens to automatic snapshots when the source disk is deleted, and apply-retention-policy keeps applying the retention window so they expire. keep-auto-snapshots is the default and is the behavior that causes the problem. Guest flush controls application-consistent snapshots, and storage location only chooses where snapshot data is stored.

question: You want to capture the boot disk of a running VM named web-golden in us-west1-a as a custom image named web-v7 in the image family web-base. Taking a short risk of an inconsistent image is acceptable, and the VM must not be stopped. Which command should you run?
options: gcloud compute images create web-v7 --source-snapshot=web-golden --source-disk-zone=us-west1-a --family=web-base --force
gcloud compute images create web-v7 --source-disk=web-golden --source-disk-zone=us-west1-a --family=web-base --force
gcloud compute machine-images create web-v7 --source-instance=web-golden --source-instance-zone=us-west1-a --family=web-base
gcloud compute disks snapshot web-golden --zone=us-west1-a --snapshot-names=web-v7 --image-family=web-base --force
explanation: By default, image creation fails when the source disk is attached to a running VM, and the --force flag lets it proceed; --family places the image in the web-base family. The --source-snapshot option expects a snapshot, not a disk name. Machine images have no image family, and disks snapshot creates a snapshot, which has no image-family flag.

question: Your instance template boots VMs from the image family app-base, and autoscaling adds new VMs all day. The newest image in the family, app-base-v12, has a bug. You want newly created VMs to use the previous image, app-base-v11, right away without editing the instance template. What should you do?
options: Run gcloud compute images update app-base-v11 --family=app-base so that it becomes the newest image in the family.
Delete the family with gcloud compute images delete app-base, then recreate it so it contains only app-base-v11.
Run gcloud compute images deprecate app-base-v12 --state=DEPRECATED so the family resolves to app-base-v11.
Create a snapshot schedule on app-base-v11 so that new VMs use the most recent snapshot of the older image.
explanation: An image family always resolves to the latest non-deprecated image in the family, so deprecating app-base-v12 makes new VMs use app-base-v11 without changing the template. Reassigning the family label does not make an older image newer. Image families are not standalone resources you delete with images delete, and snapshot schedules apply to disks, not images.

question: A zonal managed instance group named web-mig runs 10 VMs behind a load balancer. You must roll out the instance template web-tmpl-v2 to all VMs while never dropping below 10 serving VMs, creating up to 3 extra VMs at a time. Which command should you run?
options: gcloud compute instance-groups managed rolling-action start-update web-mig --version=template=web-tmpl-v2 --max-surge=0 --max-unavailable=3
gcloud compute instance-groups managed rolling-action start-update web-mig --version=template=web-tmpl-v2 --max-surge=3 --max-unavailable=0
gcloud compute instance-groups managed set-instance-template web-mig --template=web-tmpl-v2 --max-surge=3 --max-unavailable=0
gcloud compute instance-groups managed rolling-action replace web-mig --version=template=web-tmpl-v2 --max-surge=10 --max-unavailable=3
explanation: A proactive rolling update with max-unavailable=0 keeps every existing VM serving until its replacement is ready, and max-surge=3 allows up to three extra VMs at a time. Swapping the values would take three VMs out of service at once. set-instance-template has no surge flags and does not update existing VMs, and rolling-action replace recreates VMs with the current template rather than taking a new version.

question: You want to test the instance template api-tmpl-v5 on about 10% of the VMs in the managed instance group api-mig, while the rest keep running api-tmpl-v4. Which command should you run?
options: gcloud compute instance-groups managed rolling-action start-update api-mig --version=template=api-tmpl-v4 --canary-version=template=api-tmpl-v5,target-size=10%
gcloud compute instance-groups managed rolling-action start-update api-mig --version=template=api-tmpl-v5,target-size=10% --canary-version=template=api-tmpl-v4
gcloud compute instance-groups managed set-instance-template api-mig --template=api-tmpl-v5 --target-size=10% --type=opportunistic
gcloud compute instance-groups managed rolling-action start-update api-mig --version=template=api-tmpl-v5 --max-surge=10% --max-unavailable=0
explanation: A canary update keeps the current template in --version and puts the new template in --canary-version with a target-size, here 10% of the group. Reversing the two versions would leave 90% of VMs on the new template. set-instance-template has no target-size flag, and a normal rolling update with surge settings moves every VM to the new template.

question: A regional managed instance group spreads 12 VMs across three zones. You start a rolling update with --max-surge=1 --max-unavailable=0, and the request is rejected. What is the cause?
options: A rolling update cannot use max-unavailable=0 together with a surge value, so one of the two must be a percentage.
Regional MIGs do not support proactive rolling updates, so you must use an opportunistic update instead.
The surge value must be at least 10% of the group size, so a 12-VM group needs a max-surge of 2 or more.
For a regional MIG, a fixed max-surge value must be 0 or at least the number of zones, which is 3 here.
explanation: For regional MIGs, a fixed maxSurge or maxUnavailable value must be either 0 or equal to or greater than the number of zones in the group, so 1 is invalid in a three-zone group. Combining max-unavailable=0 with a surge is the normal zero-downtime pattern. Regional MIGs do support proactive updates, and there is no 10% minimum for surge.

question: You ran gcloud compute instance-groups managed set-instance-template to point the group cart-mig at a new template that changes the machine type. A day later, all the existing VMs still use the old machine type, but a VM added by a scale-out uses the new one. What explains this, and how do you update the existing VMs?
options: The autoscaler pins existing VMs to their original template; disable autoscaling for a day so the group can refresh.
Machine type changes need a regional template; recreate the template as a regional template and set it on the group again.
Setting the template only affects new VMs; start a rolling update with rolling-action start-update to apply it to existing VMs.
The new template is applied during the next maintenance window; wait for live migration to move each VM over.
explanation: set-instance-template changes the template used for new VMs in the group, but existing VMs keep their configuration until you update or recreate them, for example with rolling-action start-update. The autoscaler does not pin VMs to a template. Global templates can change machine types, and live migration never changes a VM's configuration.

question: The VM report-db in europe-west1-c is running as e2-standard-4 and needs to become e2-standard-8. You have a short maintenance window. Which sequence works?
options: Run gcloud compute instances set-machine-type report-db --machine-type=e2-standard-8 --zone=europe-west1-c --live while the VM keeps running.
Stop the VM, run gcloud compute instances set-machine-type report-db --machine-type=e2-standard-8 --zone=europe-west1-c, then start it.
Run gcloud compute instances update report-db --machine-type=e2-standard-8 --zone=europe-west1-c, then reset the VM to apply the change.
Create a snapshot of the boot disk, run gcloud compute disks resize on it with the new machine type, then restart the VM from it.
explanation: You can change the machine type only on a stopped VM, using gcloud compute instances set-machine-type, and the new type applies when you start it again. There is no --live flag for this change, and instances update does not take a machine type. Disk resizing changes storage size, not vCPUs or memory.

question: After a change to /etc/fstab, the Linux VM inv-batch no longer finishes booting, and SSH through IAP times out. The serial port output shows the boot waiting at an emergency shell. You want to log in interactively to fix the file. What should you do?
options: Run gcloud compute ssh inv-batch --tunnel-through-iap --troubleshoot to start an interactive emergency shell on the VM.
Set the metadata key serial-port-enable=TRUE on the VM, then connect with gcloud compute connect-to-serial-port inv-batch.
Run gcloud compute instances get-serial-port-output inv-batch and type commands into the output stream that the command returns.
Add an external IP address to the VM and connect with SSH, because IAP cannot reach a VM that is in emergency mode.
explanation: The interactive serial console works even when networking and the SSH daemon are not running, and you enable it with the serial-port-enable metadata key, then connect with gcloud compute connect-to-serial-port. The ssh --troubleshoot flag only diagnoses connectivity. get-serial-port-output is read-only, and an external IP does not help when sshd never starts.

question: You need a Compute Engine VM with one NVIDIA L4 GPU for an inference service. A teammate tried to create an n2-standard-8 VM with --accelerator=type=nvidia-l4,count=1, and the request failed. Which approach is correct?
options: Retry the n2-standard-8 request with --maintenance-policy=MIGRATE so that the L4 GPU can be live migrated.
Create an e2-standard-8 VM and attach the L4 GPU later with gcloud compute instances attach-disk.
Create the VM with a G2 machine type such as g2-standard-8, which comes with an L4 GPU already attached.
Create a TPU VM with gcloud compute tpus tpu-vm create and select nvidia-l4 as the accelerator type.
explanation: L4 GPUs are offered through the accelerator-optimized G2 machine series, where the GPUs are attached automatically based on the machine type. The N2 and E2 series do not support attaching GPUs, and attach-disk attaches disks, not accelerators. GPU VMs cannot live migrate, and TPU VMs use TPU accelerator types, not NVIDIA GPUs.

question: A research team wants a Cloud TPU in us-central1-b to run a JAX training job, accessed directly over SSH like a VM. Which command creates the right resource?
options: gcloud compute instances create train-tpu --zone=us-central1-b --accelerator=type=TPU_TYPE,count=1 --image-family=RUNTIME_VERSION
gcloud container node-pools create train-tpu --zone=us-central1-b --accelerator=type=TPU_TYPE --node-version=RUNTIME_VERSION
gcloud compute tpus tpu-vm create train-tpu --zone=us-central1-b --accelerator-type=TPU_TYPE --version=RUNTIME_VERSION
gcloud compute instances attach-tpu train-tpu --zone=us-central1-b --accelerator-type=TPU_TYPE --version=RUNTIME_VERSION
explanation: TPU VMs are created with gcloud compute tpus tpu-vm create, which takes the accelerator type and a TPU runtime version, and you then connect with SSH. Regular Compute Engine instances do not accept TPU types in --accelerator, and there is no attach-tpu command. A GKE node pool creates Kubernetes nodes rather than a standalone TPU VM, which the team did not ask for.

question: You just created a regional GKE cluster named shop-prod in us-central1. When you run kubectl get nodes from Cloud Shell, kubectl reports that the connection to the server localhost:8080 was refused. What should you run?
options: gcloud container clusters describe shop-prod --location=us-central1 --format=kubeconfig
kubectl config set-cluster shop-prod --server=https://us-central1.gke.googleapis.com
gcloud auth application-default login --scopes=container.clusters.get
gcloud container clusters get-credentials shop-prod --location=us-central1
explanation: The localhost:8080 error means kubectl has no kubeconfig entry for a cluster, and get-credentials writes the endpoint and credentials for shop-prod into kubeconfig. describe only prints cluster details and has no kubeconfig output format. Pointing kubectl at a made-up server URL does not authenticate it, and application default credentials do not configure kubectl.

question: A Pod named orders-7d9f-x2k is in CrashLoopBackOff. Running kubectl logs orders-7d9f-x2k shows only a few startup lines because the container has just restarted again. You need the output of the container instance that crashed. Which command should you run?
options: kubectl logs orders-7d9f-x2k --since=0s
kubectl describe pod orders-7d9f-x2k --logs
kubectl get events orders-7d9f-x2k --previous
kubectl logs orders-7d9f-x2k --previous
explanation: The --previous flag (or -p) prints the logs of the previous, terminated instance of the container, which is the one that crashed. The --since flag only limits how far back logs go for the current instance. describe has no --logs flag, and events show scheduling and restart reasons but not container output.

question: You updated the Deployment checkout three times today. Revision 5 is live and broken, and kubectl rollout history deployment/checkout shows that revision 3 was the last good one. Which command restores revision 3?
options: kubectl rollout restart deployment/checkout --revision=3
kubectl rollout undo deployment/checkout --to-revision=3
kubectl rollout history deployment/checkout --revision=3 --apply
kubectl rollout resume deployment/checkout --to-revision=3
explanation: kubectl rollout undo with --to-revision rolls the Deployment back to a specific revision from its history; without the flag it goes back only one revision, to revision 4. rollout restart re-creates Pods with the current template and has no --revision flag. rollout history only shows revisions, and rollout resume continues a paused rollout.

question: You are moving a three-node database cluster to GKE. Each replica needs its own persistent disk that stays with it when its Pod is rescheduled, and a stable network name such as db-0.db. Which Kubernetes setup should you use?
options: A StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates and a headless Service that sets clusterIP to None
A Deployment with three replicas that share one PersistentVolumeClaim and a ClusterIP Service
A DaemonSet that runs one Pod per node, using hostPath volumes and a NodePort Service
A Deployment with three replicas, emptyDir volumes and a LoadBalancer Service with session affinity
explanation: A StatefulSet gives each Pod a stable ordinal identity, and volumeClaimTemplates create one PersistentVolumeClaim per Pod that follows it across rescheduling; a headless Service provides per-Pod DNS names such as db-0.db. Deployment Pods are interchangeable and get random names. hostPath ties data to a specific node, and emptyDir is deleted when the Pod leaves the node.

question: A Service in a GKE cluster must be reachable from VMs in the same VPC but never from the internet. You want GKE to provision a Google Cloud load balancer for it. How should you configure the Service?
options: Set type: NodePort and create a VPC firewall rule that only allows traffic from the VPC address ranges.
Set type: LoadBalancer and add the annotation networking.gke.io/load-balancer-type: "Internal".
Set type: ClusterIP and add the annotation cloud.google.com/load-balancer-type: "External".
Set type: LoadBalancer and set spec.externalTrafficPolicy to Local so that only VPC clients can connect.
explanation: In GKE, a LoadBalancer Service with the networking.gke.io/load-balancer-type: "Internal" annotation provisions an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer with a private VPC address. A NodePort Service does not provision a load balancer at all. A ClusterIP Service gets no load balancer, and externalTrafficPolicy only controls how traffic is routed to nodes, not whether the address is public.

question: Your GKE Standard cluster ml-prod in us-central1 needs a new node pool for inference, with one NVIDIA L4 GPU per node and the GPU driver installed by GKE. Which command creates it?
options: gcloud container node-pools create l4-pool --cluster=ml-prod --location=us-central1 --machine-type=g2-standard-8 --accelerator=type=nvidia-l4,count=1,gpu-driver-version=default
gcloud container clusters update ml-prod --location=us-central1 --machine-type=g2-standard-8 --accelerator=type=nvidia-l4,count=1,gpu-driver-version=default
gcloud container node-pools create l4-pool --cluster=ml-prod --location=us-central1 --machine-type=n2-standard-8 --accelerator=type=nvidia-l4,count=1,gpu-driver-version=disabled
gcloud compute instances create l4-pool --location=us-central1 --machine-type=g2-standard-8 --accelerator=type=nvidia-l4,count=1 --cluster=ml-prod
explanation: GPUs are added to GKE by creating a node pool with the --accelerator flag, a GPU-capable machine type (G2 for L4), and gpu-driver-version=default so GKE installs the driver. clusters update does not create a node pool with a new machine type. N2 machines cannot use L4 GPUs and disabled skips the driver install, and standalone Compute Engine VMs do not join a GKE cluster.

question: A regional GKE cluster's node pool web-pool runs in three zones with 2 nodes per zone, 6 nodes in total. You run gcloud container clusters resize web-cluster --node-pool=web-pool --num-nodes=4 --location=us-east1. How many nodes will web-pool have when the resize finishes?
options: 4 nodes, spread across the three zones as evenly as possible
12 nodes, because the requested size applies to each of the three zones
6 nodes, because regional node pools must be resized with autoscaling
8 nodes, because the resize adds 2 more nodes to the existing total
explanation: For a node pool that spans multiple zones, --num-nodes sets the number of nodes per zone, so 4 nodes in each of three zones gives 12 nodes. The value is not a total for the whole pool, and it is not added to the current count. Regional node pools can be resized manually without autoscaling.

question: The control plane of the GKE Standard cluster pay-cluster was upgraded to a newer minor version, but the node pool batch-pool is still on the old version, and node auto-upgrade is disabled for it. You want to bring batch-pool to the control plane's version. Which command should you run?
options: gcloud container clusters upgrade pay-cluster --node-pool=batch-pool --location=europe-west1
gcloud container clusters upgrade pay-cluster --master --node-pool=batch-pool --location=europe-west1
gcloud container node-pools update batch-pool --cluster=pay-cluster --enable-autorepair --location=europe-west1
gcloud container node-pools rollback batch-pool --cluster=pay-cluster --to-version=latest --location=europe-west1
explanation: gcloud container clusters upgrade with --node-pool upgrades that node pool, and when you omit --cluster-version it defaults to the control plane's current version. The --master flag targets the control plane, which is already upgraded. Auto-repair recreates unhealthy nodes but does not change versions, and node-pools rollback reverts a failed upgrade instead of moving forward.

question: Teams set CPU and memory requests for their GKE Deployments by guessing. You want GKE to suggest request values based on observed usage, but Pods must not be evicted or changed automatically. Vertical Pod autoscaling is enabled on the cluster. What should you do?
options: Create a VerticalPodAutoscaler for each Deployment with updateMode set to "Off" and read its recommendations.
Create a HorizontalPodAutoscaler for each Deployment with a CPU target and read the suggested replica count.
Create a VerticalPodAutoscaler for each Deployment with updateMode set to "Auto" and minReplicas set to 0.
Enable node auto-provisioning so that GKE writes recommended requests into each Deployment's Pod template.
explanation: A VerticalPodAutoscaler in updateMode Off only calculates and publishes recommended requests in its status, without evicting or changing Pods. Auto mode applies the recommendations by recreating Pods, which the requirement forbids. An HPA changes replica counts rather than per-Pod requests, and node auto-provisioning creates node pools without editing workloads.

question: A Deployment has a HorizontalPodAutoscaler that targets 60% average CPU utilization. A teammate adds a VerticalPodAutoscaler in Auto mode that manages the same Deployment's CPU and memory requests. Soon the replica count and the Pod requests swing back and forth. What is the best fix?
options: Raise the HPA's maxReplicas so that it no longer reacts each time the VPA changes the Pods' CPU requests.
Change the VPA to Recreate mode, which coordinates its changes with the HPA so that the two controllers never conflict.
Do not let both act on CPU; keep the HPA on CPU and limit the VPA to memory, or scale the HPA on a custom metric.
Enable the cluster autoscaler on the node pool so that the HPA and VPA share one consistent CPU metric.
explanation: HPA utilization is measured against Pod requests, so when the VPA also changes CPU requests the two controllers react to each other; the guidance is not to use both on the same CPU or memory metric. A higher maxReplicas does not remove the feedback loop. Recreate mode still changes requests, and the cluster autoscaler adds nodes but does not coordinate the two controllers.

question: You created a HorizontalPodAutoscaler for the Deployment search with a 70% CPU utilization target. kubectl get hpa shows the target as <unknown>/70%, and the replica count never changes even under heavy load. Metrics for other workloads work. What is the most likely cause?
options: The search Deployment has fewer than three replicas, which is the minimum an HPA needs to collect metrics.
The search containers have no CPU requests set, so CPU utilization as a percentage cannot be calculated.
Cluster autoscaling is disabled on the node pool, so the HPA cannot read CPU usage from the nodes.
The HPA uses the autoscaling/v2 API, which only supports memory targets and custom metrics, not CPU.
explanation: HPA utilization targets are a percentage of each container's request, so if the containers set no CPU request the utilization is undefined and the HPA takes no action. HPAs work with any replica count within their limits. The cluster autoscaler is a separate feature from Pod metrics, and autoscaling/v2 fully supports CPU utilization targets.

question: A team deployed 40 small sidecar-style Pods to a GKE Autopilot cluster without any resource requests. The bill is much higher than expected, and kubectl describe shows that each container requests 500m CPU and 2Gi of memory. Why, and what should they do?
options: Autopilot always rounds requests up to a full node; switch the Pods to a DaemonSet so they share each node.
Autopilot copies the largest container's requests to every Pod; add limits higher than requests to stop it.
Autopilot applies default requests to containers that set none; set small explicit requests that fit the workload.
Autopilot bills for node capacity rather than requests; enable node auto-provisioning to choose smaller nodes.
explanation: When a container sets no requests, Autopilot applies the compute class defaults, which for general-purpose Pods are 0.5 vCPU and 2 GiB of memory, and Autopilot bills based on these requests. Setting explicit, smaller requests lowers cost, and Autopilot raises them only if they fall below its minimums. Autopilot does not round Pods up to whole nodes, does not copy requests between Pods, and does not bill Pods by node size.

question: You want a Pod on a GKE Autopilot cluster to run on one NVIDIA L4 GPU. Autopilot has no GPU nodes yet. What must the Pod specification include?
options: A toleration for nvidia.com/gpu and a resource request of cpu: 1, after you create an L4 node pool
A nodeSelector of cloud.google.com/gke-accelerator: nvidia-l4 and a resource limit of nvidia.com/gpu: 1
An annotation of autopilot.gke.io/gpu: nvidia-l4 and an init container that installs the NVIDIA driver
A nodeSelector of cloud.google.com/machine-family: g2 and an environment variable named NVIDIA_GPU=1
explanation: In Autopilot you request GPUs by setting the cloud.google.com/gke-accelerator nodeSelector to the GPU type and the nvidia.com/gpu resource limit to the quantity; Autopilot then provisions a GPU node and installs the driver. You do not create node pools or install drivers yourself in Autopilot. There is no autopilot.gke.io/gpu annotation, and an environment variable does not request a GPU.

question: Pods in the namespace payments use Workload Identity Federation for GKE with a Kubernetes service account bound to the IAM service account payments-app. You granted payments-app the Artifact Registry Reader role, but new Pods still fail with ImagePullBackOff and a 403 error from Artifact Registry. The node pool runs as the service account gke-nodes. What should you do?
options: Grant the Artifact Registry Reader role on the repository to gke-nodes, because image pulls use the node's service account.
Grant the Artifact Registry Writer role to payments-app, because image pulls through Workload Identity need write access.
Add the annotation iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account to the Pod spec so the kubelet pulls with payments-app.
Grant the Kubernetes service account the Storage Object Viewer role on the bucket that stores the repository.
explanation: The kubelet pulls container images using the node's IAM service account, not the Pod's Workload Identity identity, so gke-nodes needs Artifact Registry Reader on the repository. Writer access is never needed to pull. The Workload Identity annotation belongs on the Kubernetes service account and still affects only the application's API calls, and Artifact Registry access is controlled by Artifact Registry roles, not bucket roles.

question: The Deployment web reads its LOG_LEVEL setting from a ConfigMap through an environment variable. You changed the value in the ConfigMap with kubectl apply, but the running Pods still use the old value an hour later. What should you do?
options: Run kubectl rollout undo deployment/web so that the Deployment re-reads the ConfigMap's latest version.
Run kubectl annotate configmap with a sync annotation so that the kubelet pushes the change into the Pods.
Wait for the kubelet sync period, after which environment variables are refreshed inside running containers.
Run kubectl rollout restart deployment/web so that new Pods start with the updated environment variable.
explanation: Environment variables taken from a ConfigMap are set when a container starts and are not updated in running Pods, so you need new Pods, for example with kubectl rollout restart. rollout undo reverts to an older Pod template, which is not what you want. No annotation pushes new environment values into running containers; only ConfigMaps mounted as volumes are refreshed by the kubelet.

question: An application on GKE needs a database password as a Kubernetes Secret named db-creds with the key password, which its Deployment references through secretKeyRef. Which command creates the Secret?
options: kubectl create secret generic db-creds --from-literal=password='S3cure!pw'
kubectl create configmap db-creds --from-literal=password='S3cure!pw' --secret
kubectl create secret docker-registry db-creds --docker-password='S3cure!pw'
kubectl apply secret db-creds --type=Opaque --data=password='S3cure!pw'
explanation: kubectl create secret generic with --from-literal creates an Opaque Secret with the given key and value, which secretKeyRef can reference. A ConfigMap is not a Secret and has no --secret flag. The docker-registry type creates image-pull credentials with different keys, and kubectl apply works from manifests rather than taking these arguments.

question: Your GKE cluster exposes the store application through the Gateway API. You deployed store-v2 as a separate Deployment and Service next to store-v1, and want 10% of requests to reach store-v2. What should you change?
options: Scale store-v2 to one tenth of store-v1's replicas, and point both Deployments at a single Service.
Set two backendRefs in the HTTPRoute, store-v1 with weight 90 and store-v2 with weight 10.
Set a 10% maxSurge on the store-v1 Deployment's rolling update strategy and swap its image to v2.
Add a PodDisruptionBudget with maxUnavailable: 10% to store-v1 so that a share of traffic shifts.
explanation: Gateway API HTTPRoutes support weighted traffic splitting through the weight field on each backendRef, so weights of 90 and 10 send about 10% of requests to store-v2. Replica ratios behind one Service only approximate a split and change with scaling. maxSurge controls how a rolling update replaces Pods, and a PodDisruptionBudget limits voluntary evictions.

question: You deployed revision billing-00042 of the Cloud Run service billing, and it now serves 100% of traffic. Error rates are rising. The previous revision, billing-00041, was healthy. Which command restores service fastest?
options: gcloud run services update-traffic billing --to-revisions=billing-00041=100
gcloud run deploy billing --revision=billing-00041 --no-traffic --tag=rollback
gcloud run revisions delete billing-00042, which shifts its traffic to the prior revision
gcloud run services update billing --rollback --to-revision=billing-00041
explanation: update-traffic with --to-revisions immediately routes all traffic to the healthy revision without building or deploying anything. Deploying with --no-traffic would give the new revision no traffic at all. You cannot delete a revision that is serving traffic, and services update has no --rollback flag.

question: Last week you used gcloud run services update-traffic to send 100% of the Cloud Run service orders to the revision orders-00017. Today you deployed a fix with gcloud run deploy, and the deploy succeeded, but users still see the old behavior. What should you do?
options: Run gcloud run deploy orders again with --max-instances=0 so that orders-00017 is scaled down.
Delete the revision orders-00017 so that Cloud Run moves its traffic share to the newest revision.
Wait for the new revision's minimum instances to warm up, after which it receives traffic automatically.
Run gcloud run services update-traffic orders --to-latest so the latest ready revision gets all traffic.
explanation: Once traffic is pinned to a specific revision, later deployments keep that traffic split, so the new revision gets no traffic until you route it with --to-latest or --to-revisions. Max instances limits scaling and is not a way to move traffic. A revision that is serving traffic cannot be deleted, and warm-up does not change traffic assignments.

question: A Cloud Run service needs at least 3 warm instances during a product launch to avoid cold starts. You want to change this setting without deploying a new revision, and the minimum should apply across all revisions that receive traffic. Which command should you run?
options: gcloud run services update storefront --min-instances=3
gcloud run services update storefront --concurrency=3
gcloud run services update storefront --min=3
gcloud run services update-traffic storefront --min=3
explanation: The service-level --min flag sets a minimum instance count shared by all revisions receiving traffic, and it can be changed without deploying a new revision. --min-instances is a revision-level setting, so changing it creates a new revision. Concurrency controls requests per instance, and update-traffic only changes traffic assignments.

question: A legacy image-processing library used by a Cloud Run service is not thread-safe, and responses become corrupted when one instance handles several requests at once. You cannot change the code right now. What should you configure?
options: Set the service's maximum instances to 1 so that only one container handles all of the incoming requests.
Set the service's maximum concurrency to 1 so that each instance processes only one request at a time.
Set the service's minimum instances to 1 so that a warm instance is ready to process each request separately.
Enable startup CPU boost so that each request gets a dedicated vCPU while the library is processing it.
explanation: Concurrency is the maximum number of simultaneous requests one instance handles, and setting it to 1 makes Cloud Run route each request to its own instance. Max instances of 1 would push every request through one container, making the problem worse. Minimum instances only keeps instances warm, and startup CPU boost adds CPU during startup.

question: After a Cloud Run service returns its HTTP response, it sends analytics events to a third-party API in a background thread. Many of these events are never delivered, and the thread seems to stall between requests. What should you change?
options: Increase the request timeout to its maximum so that the background thread can finish before the response.
Enable startup CPU boost so that the background thread gets extra CPU after each response is returned.
Lower the maximum concurrency to 1 so that the background thread has the instance to itself between requests.
Switch the service to instance-based billing, for example with gcloud run services update --no-cpu-throttling.
explanation: With the default request-based billing, CPU is only allocated while a request is being processed, so background work after the response is throttled. Instance-based billing, set with --no-cpu-throttling, keeps CPU allocated for the instance's whole lifecycle. The request timeout limits how long a request can run, startup CPU boost only applies while an instance starts, and concurrency does not give CPU outside of requests.

question: A Cloud Run job must process 200 input files, one file per task, with no more than 20 tasks running at the same time. Each task should pick its file from the task number. Which configuration should you use?
options: Set --tasks=200 and --parallelism=20, and have the code read the CLOUD_RUN_TASK_INDEX environment variable.
Set --tasks=20 and --parallelism=200, and have the code read the CLOUD_RUN_EXECUTION environment variable.
Set --max-instances=20 and --concurrency=200, and have the code read the K_REVISION environment variable.
Set --tasks=200 and --max-retries=20, and have the code read the CLOUD_RUN_TASK_COUNT environment variable.
explanation: The task count sets how many tasks must complete, parallelism caps how many run at once, and each task gets its own CLOUD_RUN_TASK_INDEX to pick its input. Parallelism cannot exceed the task count, and the execution name does not identify a task. Max instances and concurrency are service settings, and max retries controls restarts of failed tasks rather than parallel tasks.

question: A Cloud Run service reads an API key from Secret Manager as an environment variable that references the version latest. After the security team adds a new version of the secret, some instances still use the old key for hours. You want running instances to read the newest version without redeploying. What should you do?
options: Keep the environment variable but add the version number to the secret name, so Cloud Run refreshes it.
Grant the service account the Secret Manager Admin role, so that Cloud Run can watch the secret for new versions.
Mount the secret as a volume, because Cloud Run fetches the value from Secret Manager each time the file is read.
Set the minimum instances to 0, so that each request starts a new instance that reads the newest secret version.
explanation: Secrets exposed as environment variables are resolved when an instance starts, so running instances keep the old value; a secret mounted as a volume is fetched from Secret Manager when it is read. Changing the secret name requires a redeploy and still resolves only at startup. Admin rights do not change when values are resolved, and minimum instances of 0 does not force a new instance for every request.

question: The Cloud Run service reports has 12 environment variables. You need to change only FEATURE_X to true. A colleague ran gcloud run services update reports --set-env-vars=FEATURE_X=true, and the new revision fails because the other variables are gone. Which command should have been used?
options: gcloud run services update reports --update-env-vars=FEATURE_X=true
gcloud run services update reports --env-vars-file=FEATURE_X=true
gcloud run services update reports --set-env-vars=FEATURE_X=true --keep
gcloud run services update reports --add-env-vars=FEATURE_X=true
explanation: --set-env-vars removes all existing environment variables before setting the ones you list, while --update-env-vars adds or changes only the variables you name. --env-vars-file expects a path to a YAML file rather than a key-value pair. There is no --keep or --add-env-vars flag.

question: You redeployed a Cloud Run function named resize-image, and you want only 20% of requests to reach the new revision resize-image-00008 while resize-image-00007 keeps the rest. Which command should you use?
options: gcloud functions deploy resize-image --traffic-split=resize-image-00008=20,resize-image-00007=80
gcloud run revisions update resize-image-00008 --traffic=20 --service=resize-image --keep-latest
gcloud run services update-traffic resize-image --to-revisions=resize-image-00008=20,resize-image-00007=80
gcloud eventarc triggers update resize-image --destination-run-revision=resize-image-00008 --percent=20
explanation: A Cloud Run function runs as a Cloud Run service with revisions, so you split its traffic with gcloud run services update-traffic and --to-revisions percentages. gcloud functions deploy has no --traffic-split flag, and revisions update is not a traffic command. Eventarc triggers route events to a service, not percentages of requests to revisions.

question: You create an Eventarc trigger for google.cloud.storage.object.v1.finalized events on a bucket, targeting a Cloud Run function. The trigger creation fails with a permission error about publishing to Pub/Sub. What should you grant?
options: Grant the Pub/Sub Publisher role in the project to the Cloud Storage service agent for the project.
Grant the Storage Object Viewer role on the bucket to the Eventarc trigger's service account.
Grant the Pub/Sub Subscriber role to your own user account in the project that holds the bucket.
Grant the Cloud Run Invoker role to the Cloud Storage service agent on the Cloud Run function.
explanation: Cloud Storage delivers these events through Pub/Sub, so the project's Cloud Storage service agent needs the Pub/Sub Publisher role. Object Viewer on the trigger's service account lets it read objects but does not let Storage publish notifications. Subscriber rights for your user and Invoker rights for the storage agent do not fix the publishing step.

question: A bucket named media-in is located in the europe-west1 region. You try to create an Eventarc trigger for its object-finalized events with --location=us-central1, near your Cloud Run function, and the request is rejected. What should you do?
options: Create the trigger with --location=europe-west1, the same location as the bucket, and keep the function as the destination.
Move the bucket's data to us-central1 by changing the bucket's location setting, then create the trigger in us-central1 as well.
Create the trigger with --location=global, which accepts events from Cloud Storage buckets in any region.
Create a Pub/Sub topic in us-central1 and use gcloud storage buckets update media-in --notification-topic to link it.
explanation: For Cloud Storage triggers, the bucket must be in the same project and the same region or multi-region as the Eventarc trigger, so the trigger must be created in europe-west1; it can still deliver to a function in another region. A bucket's location cannot be changed after creation. A global trigger location is not valid for Cloud Storage events, and buckets update has no notification-topic flag.

question: A Cloud Run function is triggered by object-finalized events on the bucket uploads. It creates a thumbnail and writes it back to the same bucket. Shortly after deployment, invocations and costs grow without stopping. What is the best fix?
options: Lower the function's maximum instances to 1 so that only one invocation can run at a time.
Add a retry policy to the trigger so that duplicate events are dropped after the first delivery.
Write the thumbnails to a separate bucket so that the function's output does not trigger new events.
Increase the function's timeout so each invocation finishes before the next event is delivered.
explanation: Every object the function writes into the trigger bucket produces a new finalized event, which invokes the function again in an endless loop, so writing output to another bucket breaks the cycle. Limiting instances only slows the loop. Retries resend failed events instead of dropping duplicates, and a longer timeout does not stop new events.

question: You deployed an agent to Agent Runtime on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform without specifying a custom service account. When the agent's tool queries a BigQuery dataset, the call fails with a permission denied error. Which principal should you grant the BigQuery roles to?
options: The Compute Engine default service account, PROJECT_NUMBER-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com, used by the runtime
The developer account that ran the deployment, because the deployed agent calls BigQuery with its creator's credentials
The Cloud Run service agent, service-PROJECT_NUMBER@serverless-robot-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com, which hosts agents
The AI Platform Reasoning Engine Service Agent, service-PROJECT_NUMBER@gcp-sa-aiplatform-re.iam.gserviceaccount.com
explanation: By default, agents deployed on Agent Runtime run as the AI Platform Reasoning Engine Service Agent, so that principal needs the extra BigQuery roles; you can see it in IAM by including Google-provided role grants. The Compute Engine default service account is not the agent's identity. Deployed agents do not use the deployer's credentials, and the Cloud Run service agent is not the agent's runtime identity.

question: A data scientist's Agent Platform Workbench instance needs more memory, so you want to change it from n1-standard-4 to n1-highmem-8. The instance is currently running a notebook. What should you do?
options: Change the machine type while it runs; Workbench live migrates the instance.
Create a BigQuery notebook, because Workbench instances cannot change machine type.
Stop the Workbench instance, change its machine type, and then start it again.
Resize the instance's data disk with gcloud workbench instances resize-disk.
explanation: To change the machine type or GPUs of an Agent Platform Workbench instance, you must first stop the instance, then change the hardware and start it again. Workbench does not change machine types on a running instance. Recreating the work as a BigQuery notebook is unnecessary, and resizing the data disk adds storage but not memory.

question: After you upgraded an Agent Platform Workbench instance to a newer environment version, the notebooks and data files in /home/jupyter are intact, but several Python packages that a user installed system-wide are missing. Why did this happen, and how can users avoid it next time?
options: The upgrade wipes the data disk too; users should attach a snapshot schedule to the data disk before every upgrade.
The upgrade replaces the boot disk; users should install packages with pip install --user so they live under /home/jupyter.
The upgrade disables the Python kernel; users should restart the kernel to reload their system-wide packages.
The upgrade changes the machine type; users should pin the machine type with gcloud workbench instances update.
explanation: A Workbench upgrade moves the boot disk to a new image while keeping the data disk, so anything installed outside the data disk must be reinstalled unless it was installed with --user into /home/jupyter. The data disk is preserved, which is why the notebooks survived. Restarting a kernel does not bring back deleted packages, and an upgrade does not change the machine type.

question: An analyst runs a Python notebook in BigQuery Studio on the default runtime, and pandas operations now run out of memory. You want the notebook to run on a larger machine type that the team can reuse. What should you do?
options: Increase the slot reservation assigned to the project so that the notebook's Python code gets more memory to run.
Export the notebook to a Dataproc cluster and set a larger machine type on its primary node for the pandas code.
Edit the notebook's Dataform repository settings to raise the memory limit of the compilation environment.
Create a Colab Enterprise runtime template with a larger machine type, then connect the notebook to a runtime from it.
explanation: BigQuery notebooks run on Colab Enterprise runtimes, and a runtime template defines settings such as the machine type that others can reuse when they connect a notebook to a new runtime. BigQuery slots power SQL queries, not the Python runtime. Dataproc is unnecessary here, and Dataform stores the notebook as a code asset rather than running its code.

question: You changed the machine type in a Cloud Workstations configuration from e2-standard-4 to e2-standard-8. Developers whose workstations were already running report that nothing changed. What explains this?
options: Configuration changes apply to each workstation the next time it starts, so running workstations keep the old type.
Machine type changes only apply to workstations created after the change, so existing workstations must be deleted and recreated.
Changes require a new workstation cluster, because a cluster pins the machine type for all its configurations.
The developers lack the Workstations Admin role, which is needed to receive updated configuration settings.
explanation: Updates to a workstation configuration apply to existing workstations automatically when they next start, so running workstations keep their old machine type until they are stopped and started again. Existing workstations do not need to be deleted. Machine type is part of the configuration, not the cluster, and developers do not need admin rights to pick up configuration changes.

question: Developers on Cloud Workstations install extra CLI tools with apt-get each morning because the tools disappear after the workstation restarts. Files they keep in their home directories survive restarts. You want the tools to always be present. What should you do?
options: Increase the size of the persistent home disk in the workstation configuration so that packages installed with apt-get are kept.
Set the configuration's idle timeout to 0 so that workstations never stop and the installed tools stay in place.
Take a snapshot of a workstation's boot disk after the tools are installed and set it as the default boot image.
Build a custom container image with the tools, push it to Artifact Registry, and set it in the workstation configuration.
explanation: Only the persistent home directory survives a restart; the rest of the file system comes from the configuration's container image, so tools should be baked into a custom image stored in Artifact Registry. A larger home disk does not keep system-level installs outside /home. Disabling the idle timeout only delays the loss and wastes money, and the workstation environment comes from the configuration's container image, not from a disk snapshot.

question: A build server writes a static website to /var/www/build. After each build, the bucket gs://site-assets must contain exactly the same files as the directory, including removing objects whose source files were deleted locally. Which command should you run?
options: gcloud storage rsync /var/www/build gs://site-assets --recursive --delete-unmatched-destination-objects
gcloud storage rsync /var/www/build gs://site-assets --recursive --checksums-only --no-clobber
gcloud storage mv /var/www/build gs://site-assets --recursive --no-clobber --delete-unmatched-destination-objects
gcloud storage cp /var/www/build gs://site-assets --recursive --no-clobber --continue-on-error
explanation: rsync with --recursive copies new and changed files, and --delete-unmatched-destination-objects removes destination objects that no longer exist in the source, which makes the bucket an exact mirror. cp with --no-clobber never deletes anything, --checksums-only only changes how files are compared, and mv has no such flag and would remove the local files.

question: A team uploaded 2 TB of log archives to a Coldline bucket. Twenty days later they ran gcloud storage mv to rename every object to a new prefix in the same bucket. The next invoice shows unexpected retrieval and early deletion charges. What explains these charges?
options: Renaming objects re-enabled Autoclass on the bucket, which moved the objects back to Standard and billed a class transition fee for each object
Coldline objects cannot be renamed in place, so gcloud downloaded every object to the client machine and uploaded it again, which was billed as retrieval
mv performs an atomic server-side rename, but Cloud Storage bills every rename of a Coldline object as network egress between storage locations
mv copies each object to the new name and then deletes the source, so Coldline retrieval fees and early deletion charges for the unmet minimum duration apply
explanation: gcloud storage mv is not atomic: it copies each object to the destination and then removes the source. Reading a Coldline object incurs retrieval fees, and deleting it before its 90-day minimum incurs an early deletion charge for the remaining days. It is not billed as egress, does not involve Autoclass, and a bucket-to-bucket or in-bucket move does not route data through the client.

question: The bucket gs://app-config has Object Versioning enabled. You want each object to keep its live version plus the two most recent noncurrent versions, and older noncurrent versions should be deleted automatically. Which lifecycle rule should you add?
options: {"action": {"type": "Delete"}, "condition": {"isLive": false, "numNewerVersions": 3}}
{"action": {"type": "Delete"}, "condition": {"isLive": false, "daysSinceNoncurrentTime": 2}}
{"action": {"type": "Delete"}, "condition": {"isLive": true, "numNewerVersions": 3}}
{"action": {"type": "Delete"}, "condition": {"isLive": false, "numNewerVersions": 2}}
explanation: numNewerVersions counts all newer versions including the live one, so a version with 3 or more newer versions is the third-oldest noncurrent version or older; deleting those keeps the live version and two noncurrent versions. A value of 2 would also delete the second most recent noncurrent version, daysSinceNoncurrentTime is time-based rather than count-based, and isLive true targets live objects.

question: An application uploads large files to gs://media-ingest with the XML API multipart upload feature. Some uploads are abandoned and never completed, and their uploaded parts keep adding to the storage bill. You want parts of uploads that are still incomplete after 7 days removed automatically. What should you configure?
options: A soft delete duration of 7 days so that abandoned parts are purged when the duration expires
A lifecycle rule with the SetStorageClass action to ARCHIVE and an age condition of 7 on the bucket
A lifecycle rule with the AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload action and an age condition of 7
A lifecycle rule with the Delete action and the conditions isLive false and age 7 on the bucket
explanation: The AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload lifecycle action aborts incomplete multipart uploads and deletes their parts, and it supports the age, matchesPrefix and matchesSuffix conditions. Incomplete parts are not live or noncurrent objects, so a Delete rule on noncurrent versions does not touch them, changing class would still bill for them, and soft delete only retains data after deletion.

question: A bucket has this lifecycle rule: action SetStorageClass to NEARLINE, condition matchesStorageClass COLDLINE and age 30. The goal is to move older Coldline objects to Nearline because they are read again often. A week after adding the rule, no object has changed class. What is the reason?
options: Lifecycle configuration changes can take up to 30 days to take effect, so the rule has not yet been evaluated against existing objects
The matchesStorageClass condition can only be combined with the Delete action, so the SetStorageClass action is silently ignored
SetStorageClass rules only apply to buckets with Object Versioning enabled, and this bucket stores only live object versions
Lifecycle rules cannot move objects to a warmer class, so a Coldline to Nearline transition never occurs
explanation: SetStorageClass only supports transitions to colder classes, and Coldline can only move to Archive; unsupported transitions are not validated and simply do not occur. To move objects to Nearline you rewrite them, for example with gcloud storage objects update and --storage-class. Rule changes take effect within about 24 hours, matchesStorageClass works with SetStorageClass, and versioning is not required.

question: An object is uploaded to a bucket whose default class is Nearline (30-day minimum). On day 10, a lifecycle rule changes it to Coldline (90-day minimum). On day 95 after upload, a user deletes it. Which early deletion charges apply?
options: A Coldline early deletion charge for 5 days, because the 90-day Coldline minimum restarts when the class change happens
A Nearline early deletion charge for 20 days, billed when the lifecycle rule moved the object out of Nearline on day 10
None, because lifecycle class changes have no early deletion fee and 95 days since creation exceed 90
Both a 20-day Nearline charge at the transition and a 5-day Coldline charge at deletion, because each class bills its own minimum
explanation: Lifecycle SetStorageClass transitions carry no early deletion fee, and the time an object spent in its original class counts toward the new class's minimum storage duration. Because age is measured from creation, the object was 95 days old at deletion, which exceeds Coldline's 90-day minimum. The minimum does not restart at the transition, so neither partial charge applies.

question: The bucket gs://ops-config has Object Versioning enabled. A deployment script overwrote config.yaml with a broken file an hour ago. You need the previous content to become the live config.yaml again. What should you do?
options: Run gcloud storage objects update gs://ops-config/config.yaml --versioning to promote the newest noncurrent version automatically
List versions with gcloud storage ls -a, then gcloud storage cp the older generation over the live config.yaml
Run gcloud storage restore gs://ops-config/config.yaml#GENERATION to bring back the noncurrent version as a soft-deleted object restore
Run gcloud storage buckets update gs://ops-config --no-versioning, which rolls each object back to its previous version
explanation: With versioning, the overwritten content is kept as a noncurrent generation; listing with -a shows the generation numbers, and copying gs://ops-config/config.yaml#GENERATION onto gs://ops-config/config.yaml makes it live again. gcloud storage restore is for soft-deleted objects, not noncurrent versions. Disabling versioning does not roll anything back, and objects update has no versioning flag.

question: A bucket without Object Versioning uses the default soft delete policy. Three days ago an engineer deleted gs://finance-data/q3-report.csv by mistake. You need to recover it. What should you do?
options: Nothing can be recovered, because soft delete only protects objects that were overwritten and not objects that were deleted
List with gcloud storage ls --soft-deleted, then run gcloud storage restore with the object's generation
Enable Object Versioning on the bucket now, which converts recently deleted objects into noncurrent versions you can copy back
Find the generation with gcloud storage ls -a, then copy gs://finance-data/q3-report.csv#GENERATION over the deleted object name
explanation: Soft delete is on by default with a 7-day retention, so an object deleted three days ago is still retained in a soft-deleted state. You list soft-deleted objects with gcloud storage ls --soft-deleted and restore with gcloud storage restore, optionally naming the generation. The -a listing shows noncurrent versions, not soft-deleted ones, and enabling versioning afterwards does not affect objects already deleted.

question: A scratch bucket stores about 200 GB of temporary files that a batch job deletes and rewrites every hour. The live data size is stable, but billed storage for the bucket is many times higher than 200 GB. The data never needs to be recovered. What should you do to reduce the cost?
options: Disable soft delete on the bucket with gcloud storage buckets update gs://scratch --clear-soft-delete
Disable Object Versioning on the bucket with gcloud storage buckets update gs://scratch --no-versioning
Add a lifecycle rule that deletes objects at age 1 with gcloud storage buckets update --lifecycle-file
Enable Autoclass on the bucket with gcloud storage buckets update gs://scratch --enable-autoclass
explanation: Soft delete retains deleted and overwritten objects for the retention duration, 7 days by default, and those soft-deleted objects keep accruing storage charges. With hourly rewrites, the retained copies far exceed the live data, so clearing the soft delete policy removes the cost for data that never needs recovery. Versioning is not the cause here, Autoclass changes classes rather than retention, and a lifecycle Delete creates more soft-deleted objects.

question: Regulators require that trade records in gs://trade-records cannot be deleted or overwritten for 7 years after they are written, and that no one, including project owners, can shorten or remove this protection later. What should you do?
options: Set a retention policy with --retention-period=7y, then lock it with gcloud storage buckets update gs://trade-records --lock-retention-period
Enable Object Versioning and a lifecycle rule that deletes noncurrent versions only after 7 years, then enable uniform bucket-level access
Set a retention policy with --retention-period=7y and remove the storage.objects.delete permission from every role used in the project
Enable a default event-based hold on the bucket and add an IAM deny policy that blocks storage.buckets.update for all principals in the organization
explanation: A retention policy blocks deletion and overwrite until each object reaches the retention period, and locking it is irreversible: a locked policy can be increased but never reduced or removed.
