An unlocked policy can still be shortened or cleared by anyone with bucket update permission. Versioning keeps old copies but allows deletion, and holds plus IAM controls can be changed by administrators.

question: Your organization blocks service account key creation. You run gcloud storage sign-url gs://reports/q3.pdf --duration=3d --impersonate-service-account=signer@prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com for a partner without a Google account, and the command rejects the duration. What should you do?
options: Change the flag to --duration=72h, because the command rejects the day unit and only accepts durations written in hours
Grant the partner's email address the Storage Object Viewer role on the object, because signed URLs cannot exceed one day
Add --private-key-file with a newly created key for the service account, because key-signed URLs can be valid for 7 days
Issue a URL with --duration=12h and generate a new one when needed, because impersonation-signed URLs are limited to 12 hours
explanation: When gcloud storage sign-url signs through impersonation, the system-managed key limits the URL to at most 12 hours; 7 days is only available when signing with a private key file or an activated service account. Writing 72h is still three days. A new key violates the organization's key restriction, and an IAM grant does not work for someone without a Google account.

question: A supplier without a Google account must upload one file, gs://supplier-drop/inbound/prices.csv, within the next two hours. Nobody else should gain write access to the bucket. You can impersonate the service account uploader@prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com. Which command should you run?
options: gcloud storage sign-url gs://supplier-drop/inbound/prices.csv --http-verb=PUT --duration=2h --impersonate-service-account=uploader@prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com
gcloud storage sign-url gs://supplier-drop/inbound/prices.csv --http-verb=GET --duration=2h --impersonate-service-account=uploader@prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com
gcloud storage sign-url gs://supplier-drop/inbound/ --http-verb=PUT --duration=2h --impersonate-service-account=uploader@prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com
gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding gs://supplier-drop --member=allUsers --role=roles/storage.objectCreator for the two-hour window
explanation: A signed URL created with --http-verb=PUT authorizes exactly one upload operation on the named object for the stated duration, with no Google account needed. A GET URL only allows downloads, and granting allUsers object creation opens the bucket to everyone. sign-url does not support signing a directory-style prefix, so the URL must name the object.

question: The bucket gs://shared-docs has uniform bucket-level access enabled. An older application that sets object ACLs to give each team access to its own prefix now fails with 400 errors. Each team must still be limited to its own prefix. What should you do?
options: Disable uniform bucket-level access and have the application keep setting object ACLs on every new upload
Create a managed folder for each team's prefix and grant that team's group IAM roles on its managed folder
Grant every team the Storage Legacy Object Reader role on the bucket so the old ACL calls start succeeding
Upload objects with --predefined-acl=projectPrivate so that each team's objects inherit the right access
explanation: With uniform bucket-level access, ACLs are disabled and access comes only from IAM, so ACL calls fail with 400 Bad Request. Managed folders let you attach IAM policies to a prefix, which gives each team scoped access without ACLs. Predefined ACLs are also ACLs, legacy roles do not re-enable ACLs, and disabling uniform access is blocked after 90 days and is often forbidden by organization policy.

question: You upload 500 GB to a Nearline bucket. Nearline storage costs $0.010 per GB per month and has a 30-day minimum storage duration. You delete all the data after 10 days. Ignoring operations and retrieval fees, about how much will storing this data cost in total?
options: $3.33, because the early deletion charge covers the remaining 20 days and the 10 days stored are waived
$5.00, since 10 days of storage plus early deletion for the other 20 days equals 30 days
$10.00, because early deletion bills the stored days plus another full 30-day minimum as a deletion penalty
$1.67, because Nearline storage is prorated and bills only for the 10 days that the data was actually stored
explanation: Deleting Nearline data before 30 days incurs an early deletion charge equal to storage for the remaining days, so the total equals 30 days of storage: 500 GB x $0.010 = $5.00. The 10 stored days are about $1.67 and the early deletion charge for 20 days is about $3.33, and they are added together. There is no second minimum-duration penalty.

question: A bucket holds 2,000 GB in Archive storage in us-central1. Archive retrieval costs $0.05 per GB. An analyst copies 400 GB of it to a Compute Engine VM in us-central1 for a one-time investigation. Ignoring operation charges, what retrieval cost and access time should you expect?
options: About $20 in retrieval fees, and the data is readable within milliseconds like any other storage class
No retrieval fee because the VM is in the same region, but the data needs up to 12 hours to be restored
About $20 in retrieval fees, plus a restore request that takes several hours before the objects are readable
About $100 in retrieval fees, because Archive bills retrieval on the whole bucket when any object is read
explanation: Retrieval fees are charged per GB read, so 400 GB x $0.05 = $20; reading in the same region avoids egress but not retrieval fees. All Cloud Storage classes, including Archive, return data with millisecond latency, so there is no restore step or multi-hour delay. Retrieval is not billed on the entire bucket.

question: Reporting queries are slowing down the Cloud SQL for MySQL instance orders-primary in us-central1. You want a read-only copy in europe-west1 for analysts there, kept up to date by replication. Which command should you run?
options: gcloud sql instances patch orders-primary --availability-type=regional --secondary-zone=europe-west1-b
gcloud sql instances create orders-eu-replica --master-instance-name=orders-primary --region=europe-west1
gcloud sql backups restore latest --restore-instance=orders-eu-replica --backup-instance=orders-primary
gcloud sql instances clone orders-primary orders-eu-replica --point-in-time=2026-11-18T09:00:00Z
explanation: Creating an instance with --master-instance-name makes it a read replica of that primary, and --region places it in another region as a cross-region replica. Making the primary regional adds an HA standby in the same region that does not serve reads. A clone or a backup restore produces an independent copy that does not stay in sync.

question: The Cloud SQL instance billing-db must not receive any maintenance during the retail freeze from 20 November 2026 to 5 January 2027. Maintenance is otherwise allowed in the configured Sunday window. Which command should you run?
options: gcloud sql instances patch billing-db --maintenance-window-day=SUN --maintenance-window-hour=3 --maintenance-release-channel=production --no-backup
gcloud sql instances patch billing-db --maintenance-window-any --deny-maintenance-period-time=00:00:00 --activation-policy=ALWAYS
gcloud sql instances patch billing-db --deny-maintenance-period-start-date=2026-11-20 --deny-maintenance-period-end-date=2027-01-05 --deny-maintenance-period-time=00:00:00
gcloud sql instances patch billing-db --maintenance-release-channel=preview --maintenance-window-day=SAT --maintenance-window-hour=0
explanation: A deny maintenance period blocks maintenance between a start and end date, and Cloud SQL allows a period of 1 to 90 days, so a 47-day freeze fits. Changing the window day or hour, or the release channel, only changes when maintenance happens. --maintenance-window-any removes the user-defined window instead of blocking maintenance.

question: You must inspect the data in last night's automated backup of the production Cloud SQL instance orders-prod without changing orders-prod. You have created an empty instance named orders-check with a compatible configuration. What should you do?
options: Run gcloud sql export sql orders-prod gs://audit-bucket/dump.sql and import that file into orders-check
Run gcloud sql instances promote-replica orders-check after starting replication from the orders-prod backup
Run gcloud sql backups restore BACKUP_ID --restore-instance=orders-check --backup-instance=orders-prod
Run gcloud sql backups restore BACKUP_ID --restore-instance=orders-prod during the next maintenance window
explanation: Restoring a backup overwrites all data on the target instance, so you restore to the separate instance orders-check and name the source with --backup-instance. Restoring onto orders-prod would replace production data. An export captures the current data rather than last night's backup, and promoting a replica has nothing to do with restoring a backup.

question: A Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL Enterprise edition instance has point-in-time recovery enabled. Auditors want you to be able to recover to any moment in the past 14 days. Running gcloud sql instances patch with --retained-transaction-log-days=14 fails. What should you do?
options: Upgrade the instance to Enterprise Plus edition, which supports up to 35 days of transaction log retention
Enable binary logging on the instance first, because transaction log days can only be set after it is on
Set --retained-backups-count=14 instead, because PITR retention follows the number of daily backups kept
Move the transaction logs to Cloud Storage with a lifecycle rule that keeps each log object for 14 days
explanation: For Enterprise edition instances, transaction log retention for point-in-time recovery defaults to and is capped at 7 days, while Enterprise Plus allows up to 35 days. The retained backups count controls daily backups, not the PITR window. Binary logging is the MySQL mechanism, and Cloud SQL does not let you manage its transaction logs with bucket lifecycle rules.

question: A new compliance rule requires the existing Cloud SQL instance crm-db to be encrypted with a customer-managed key from Cloud KMS. The instance currently uses Google-managed encryption. What should you do?
options: Rotate the Google-managed key for crm-db in the Cloud KMS console, which converts it to a customer-managed key
Create a new instance with --disk-encryption-key set to the KMS key, migrate the data to it, and then retire crm-db
Run gcloud sql instances patch crm-db --disk-encryption-key with the KMS key and restart the instance afterwards
Set an organization policy that requires CMEK, which re-encrypts crm-db with the key during the next maintenance
explanation: Cloud SQL CMEK can only be configured when an instance is created, so an existing Google-encrypted instance must be replaced by a new CMEK instance and the data moved over. The patch command has no disk encryption key option. Google-managed keys are not visible for you to rotate, and a CMEK organization policy restricts new resources rather than re-encrypting existing ones.

question: The Spanner database ledger in instance prod-sp has version_retention_period set to 7d. A faulty job corrupted rows three hours ago. You need a full copy of the database as it was just before the job, without changing the live database. What should you do?
options: Export the database to Cloud Storage now with Dataflow and edit the exported files to remove the rows from the job
Lower version_retention_period to 3h with a DDL statement so that Spanner discards the versions written after the job
Run gcloud spanner databases restore with the live database as the source and --destination-database=ledger to roll it back
Create a backup with gcloud spanner backups create and --version-time set before the job, then restore it to a new database
explanation: With a 7-day version retention period, Spanner can create a backup whose --version-time is an earlier timestamp, giving a consistent copy from just before the job. You then restore that backup to a new database. Spanner restores always go to a new database rather than rolling back an existing one, shrinking retention does not undo writes, and exporting now captures the corrupted data.

question: The AlloyDB cluster sales-prod in us-east4 has continuous backup and recovery enabled. A table was dropped at 10:42 UTC today. You need the data as it was at 10:40 UTC while sales-prod keeps serving traffic. Which command should you run?
options: gcloud alloydb backups create sales-recover --region=us-east4 --cluster=sales-prod --point-in-time=2026-11-18T10:40:00Z
gcloud alloydb clusters restore sales-recover --region=us-east4 --source-cluster=sales-prod --point-in-time=2026-11-18T10:40:00Z
gcloud alloydb instances restart sales-primary --region=us-east4 --cluster=sales-prod --point-in-time=2026-11-18T10:40:00Z
gcloud alloydb clusters restore sales-prod --region=us-east4 --source-cluster=sales-prod --point-in-time=2026-11-18T10:40:00Z
explanation: AlloyDB point-in-time recovery creates a new cluster from a source cluster and a timestamp, so restoring into sales-recover leaves sales-prod untouched and you can copy the table back. You cannot restore into the existing cluster's name. Creating a backup captures the current state, and restarting an instance has no point-in-time option.

question: Your Firestore database has point-in-time recovery enabled. Analysts need a consistent export of the whole database as it was at 09:00 UTC yesterday, written to gs://fs-exports. Which command should you run?
options: gcloud firestore databases restore --destination-database=fs-exports --snapshot-time=2026-11-17T09:00:00Z
gcloud firestore export gs://fs-exports/2026-11-17 --snapshot-time=2026-11-17T09:00:00Z
gcloud firestore import gs://fs-exports/2026-11-17 --snapshot-time=2026-11-17T09:00:00Z
gcloud firestore export gs://fs-exports/2026-11-17 --async --collection-ids=all-collections
explanation: The --snapshot-time flag of gcloud firestore export exports a consistent view of the database at a past whole-minute timestamp within the retained version window, which PITR extends to 7 days. A plain export reads current data with no consistency guarantee and collection IDs only filter collection groups. Import loads data rather than exporting it, and databases restore works from backups and has no snapshot-time flag.

question: A bad batch job overwrote cells in the Bigtable table events in instance prod-bt. A backup named events-bkp exists on cluster prod-bt-c1. You want the backed-up data available alongside the current table so that engineers can compare them. Which command should you run?
options: gcloud bigtable backups create events-restored --instance=prod-bt --cluster=prod-bt-c1 --table=events --retention-period=7d --async
gcloud bigtable instances tables restore --source-instance=prod-bt --source-cluster=prod-bt-c1 --source=events-bkp --destination-instance=prod-bt --destination=events-restored
gcloud bigtable instances tables restore --source-instance=prod-bt --source-cluster=prod-bt-c1 --source=events --destination-instance=prod-bt --destination=events-bkp
gcloud bigtable instances tables restore --source-instance=prod-bt --source-cluster=prod-bt-c1 --source=events-bkp --destination-instance=prod-bt --destination=events
explanation: Bigtable restores a backup into a new table, so naming events-bkp as the source and events-restored as the destination puts the old data next to the current table. Creating a backup would capture the already-damaged data, and the source must be the backup rather than the table. The destination cannot be the existing events table, because restore does not overwrite a table in place.

question: An analyst will run a dashboard query 5 times per day. A dry run of the query reports that it will process 4 TiB. The project uses on-demand pricing at $6.25 per TiB scanned, and results are not cached between runs. What is the approximate daily query cost?
options: $0, because a query that was validated with a dry run is not billed when it runs later
$25, because the dry run total already includes every run scheduled for the same day
$125, because each run bills 4 TiB at $6.25 per TiB and the query runs five times each day
$31.25, because on-demand pricing bills the first run in full and later runs at a quarter
explanation: On-demand pricing bills bytes processed per query: 4 TiB x $6.25 = $25 per run, and five uncached runs cost $125 per day. A dry run estimates a single execution and is itself free, but it does not make later runs free. There is no discount for repeated runs other than cached results, which the stem rules out.

question: Developers sometimes run ad hoc queries that scan far more data than intended. You want any single query that would bill more than 1 TB to fail before incurring charges, without changing reservations. Which flag should be used with bq query?
options: --dry_run --use_legacy_sql=false --nouse_cache
--priority=BATCH --use_legacy_sql=false
--maximum_bytes_billed=1000000000000
explanation: --maximum_bytes_billed sets an upper limit on bytes billed for the query; if the estimate exceeds the limit, the query fails without being charged. --dry_run only validates and estimates, so the query never actually runs. --max_rows limits displayed result rows rather than bytes scanned, and batch priority changes scheduling, not cost.

question: A BigQuery load job submitted by a scheduled script failed overnight. You have the job ID and need to see its final state and the error message returned by BigQuery. Which command should you run?
options: bq show -j JOB_ID
bq head -j JOB_ID
bq cancel JOB_ID
gcloud dataflow jobs describe JOB_ID
explanation: bq show -j displays the job resource, including its status, the error result and any additional errors. bq head reads table rows or query results rather than job errors, and bq cancel requests cancellation of a running job. gcloud dataflow jobs describe is for Dataflow jobs, not BigQuery jobs.

question: The ingestion-time partitioned table analytics.clickstream grows every day. Policy says each day's partition must be deleted 90 days after its partition date, while the table itself must remain. Which command should you run?
options: bq update --default_table_expiration=7776000 analytics
bq update --time_partitioning_expiration=90 --time_partitioning_type=DAY analytics.clickstream
bq update --expiration=7776000 analytics.clickstream
bq update --time_partitioning_expiration=7776000 analytics.clickstream
explanation: --time_partitioning_expiration sets, in seconds, how long each partition is kept after its partition time, and 90 days is 7,776,000 seconds. --expiration would delete the entire table 90 days from now, and a dataset default table expiration applies only to newly created tables. A value of 90 is interpreted as 90 seconds.

question: A company runs large BigQuery workloads every day, and finance wants query costs to be predictable from month to month instead of varying with the bytes each query scans. What should you recommend?
options: Keep on-demand pricing and set table expiration on all datasets so that less stored data is scanned
Use capacity-based pricing with a BigQuery edition slot reservation assigned to the project
Keep on-demand pricing and require every analyst to run a dry run before each query to estimate its cost
Move the tables to long-term storage pricing, which also lowers and fixes the cost of querying them
explanation: Capacity-based pricing charges for slot capacity from a BigQuery edition reservation rather than bytes scanned, which makes query spending predictable. Dry runs only estimate on-demand cost, and expiration reduces storage rather than fixing query spend. Long-term storage pricing applies to storage of unmodified tables and does not change query pricing.

question: A streaming Dataflow job in us-central1 reads from Pub/Sub and writes to BigQuery. You must stop it for a schema change, and any data already read into the pipeline must still be written before it stops. Which command should you run?
options: gcloud dataflow jobs drain JOB_ID --region=us-central1
gcloud dataflow jobs cancel JOB_ID --region=us-central1
gcloud dataflow jobs list --status=active --region=us-central1
gcloud dataflow jobs describe JOB_ID --region=us-central1
explanation: Draining stops the job from reading new input while it finishes processing elements already in the pipeline, so no in-flight data is lost. Cancel stops the job immediately and can discard buffered data. Listing and describing jobs only show status and do not stop anything.

question: Subscribers on the pull subscription orders-sub take about 90 seconds to process each message. The subscription uses the default acknowledgement deadline, and many messages are being delivered more than once while they are still being processed. What should you do?
options: Run gcloud pubsub subscriptions update orders-sub --retain-acked-messages
Run gcloud pubsub subscriptions update orders-sub --message-retention-duration=120s
Run gcloud pubsub subscriptions update orders-sub --min-retry-delay=120s
Run gcloud pubsub subscriptions update orders-sub --ack-deadline=120
explanation: The default acknowledgement deadline is 10 seconds, so Pub/Sub redelivers messages that are still being worked on; raising it above the processing time stops these duplicates. The minimum retry delay only applies to a retry policy after a nack or deadline expiry, and the retention settings control how long messages are kept, not when they are redelivered.

question: You set the dead-letter topic orders-dlq on the subscription orders-sub with a maximum of 10 delivery attempts. Messages that fail repeatedly are still redelivered indefinitely and never reach orders-dlq. Both resources are in the same project. What is the most likely fix?
options: Lower the maximum delivery attempts to 1 so that the first failed delivery forwards the message
Enable retained acknowledged messages on orders-sub so that failed messages can be forwarded
Grant the Pub/Sub service agent Publisher on orders-dlq and Subscriber on orders-sub
Grant the subscriber application's service account the Publisher role on the orders-dlq topic
explanation: Pub/Sub forwards undeliverable messages itself, using the Pub/Sub service agent of the project, which needs permission to publish to the dead-letter topic and to subscribe to the source subscription to acknowledge forwarded messages. The subscriber application does not forward messages. The maximum delivery attempts must be between 5 and 100, and retaining acked messages is unrelated to dead-lettering.

question: A bug in a subscriber corrupted every message it processed and acknowledged since 06:00 UTC today. The subscription orders-sub was created with --retain-acked-messages and a 7-day retention duration. After deploying a fix, you need those messages delivered again. Which command should you run?
options: gcloud pubsub subscriptions seek orders-sub --time=2026-11-18T06:00:00Z
gcloud pubsub subscriptions update orders-sub --ack-deadline=600
gcloud pubsub snapshots create replay-0600 --subscription=orders-sub
gcloud pubsub subscriptions modify-message-ack-deadline orders-sub --ack-deadline=0
explanation: Seeking a subscription to a timestamp marks retained messages published after that time as unacknowledged, so they are redelivered; this works for acknowledged messages because the subscription retains them. A snapshot created now only captures the current backlog state. Changing or resetting the ack deadline does not affect messages that were already acknowledged.

question: Database Center flagged a Cloud SQL instance for missing automated backups. You enabled automated backups on the instance an hour ago, but Database Center still shows the issue. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Database Center only clears an issue after you acknowledge it by opening it in Gemini chat
The instance must be restarted before Database Center can detect that backups are enabled
Database Center data is not real time and can take up to 24 hours to refresh
Database Center checks backups only for AlloyDB and Spanner, so the Cloud SQL flag is stale
explanation: Database Center aggregates fleet data that usually updates within minutes but can take up to 24 hours, so a recently fixed issue may still appear for a while. Issues do not require acknowledgement in Gemini chat, enabling backups does not require a restart, and Database Center reports data protection issues for Cloud SQL as well as other engines.

question: You set a Cloud KMS key as the default encryption key for gs://hr-records. New uploads are encrypted with the key, but objects that existed before the change are still encrypted with Google-managed keys. The policy requires all objects to use the new key. What should you do?
options: Rewrite the existing objects with gcloud storage objects update gs://hr-records --recursive --encryption-key=KEY_NAME
Wait 24 hours, because Cloud Storage re-encrypts existing objects in the background after the default changes
Run gcloud storage buckets update gs://hr-records --default-encryption-key=KEY_NAME again with --recursive
Disable uniform bucket-level access so that the default key setting is allowed to propagate to old objects
explanation: A bucket default key applies only to objects written after it is set, so existing objects must be rewritten with the key, for example with gcloud storage objects update and --encryption-key. Cloud Storage does not re-encrypt existing objects in the background, buckets update has no recursive re-encryption option, and uniform bucket-level access is unrelated to encryption.

question: The VM legacy-ftp in us-central1-a uses the ephemeral external IP 34.123.45.67, which several partners have allowlisted. You must keep this exact address even if the VM is stopped or recreated. Which command should you run?
options: gcloud compute instances add-access-config legacy-ftp --zone=us-central1-a --address=34.123.45.67
gcloud compute addresses create ftp-ip --addresses=34.123.45.67 --global --ip-version=IPV4
gcloud compute addresses create ftp-ip --region=us-central1 --network-tier=PREMIUM --subnet=default
gcloud compute addresses create ftp-ip --addresses=34.123.45.67 --region=us-central1
explanation: Running gcloud compute addresses create with --addresses and the VM's region promotes the in-use ephemeral external IP to a regional static address. A VM's external IP is regional, so --global is wrong, and creating an address without --addresses reserves a new IP. Adding another access config does not reserve the existing address.

question: A database VM in us-east1 must always use the internal IP 10.40.0.50 from the subnet data-subnet, so that application configuration never changes when the VM is recreated. What should you do first?
options: Run gcloud compute addresses create db-ip --region=us-east1 --network-tier=STANDARD --addresses=10.40.0.50
Run gcloud compute addresses create db-ip --region=us-east1 --subnet=data-subnet --addresses=10.40.0.50
Run gcloud compute addresses create db-ip --global --purpose=VPC_PEERING --addresses=10.40.0.50 --prefix-length=32
Run gcloud compute networks subnets update data-subnet --region=us-east1 --add-secondary-ranges=db=10.40.0.50/32
explanation: Reserving a regional address with --subnet creates a static internal IP from that subnet, and --addresses picks the specific address; you then assign it to the VM's network interface. VPC_PEERING ranges are for private services access, a network tier applies to external addresses, and a secondary range does not reserve an address for a VM.

question: In a VPC, route A sends 10.0.0.0/8 to a Cloud VPN tunnel with priority 100. Route B sends 10.20.0.0/16 to an appliance VM with priority 1000. Neither route has tags. Which path does traffic from a VM to 10.20.5.9 take?
options: Route B, because the most specific destination prefix is chosen before priority is compared
Route A, because a lower priority number always wins regardless of the destination prefix
Both routes, because Google Cloud splits traffic across routes that match the same destination
Neither route, because overlapping static routes in one VPC are rejected when they are created
explanation: Google Cloud selects routes by longest prefix match first, and priority only breaks ties between routes with the same destination prefix length. The /16 route is more specific than the /8 route, so traffic to 10.20.5.9 goes to the appliance. ECMP applies only to routes with the same prefix and priority, and overlapping static routes are allowed.

question: Two firewall appliance VMs sit behind an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer whose forwarding rule is fw-ilb-fr in us-central1. All traffic from the VPC shared-vpc to 172.16.0.0/12 must go through the appliances, with failover handled by the load balancer. Which command should you run?
options: gcloud compute routes create to-onprem --network=shared-vpc --destination-range=172.16.0.0/12 --next-hop-vpn-tunnel=fw-ilb-fr --next-hop-vpn-tunnel-region=us-central1
gcloud compute routes create to-onprem --network=shared-vpc --destination-range=172.16.0.0/12 --next-hop-gateway=fw-ilb-fr --priority=100
gcloud compute routes create to-onprem --network=shared-vpc --destination-range=172.16.0.0/12 --next-hop-ilb=fw-ilb-fr --next-hop-ilb-region=us-central1
gcloud compute routes create to-onprem --network=shared-vpc --destination-range=172.16.0.0/12 --next-hop-instance=fw-ilb-fr --next-hop-instance-zone=us-central1-a
explanation: --next-hop-ilb takes the name or IP of an internal passthrough load balancer's forwarding rule, so traffic is spread across healthy appliances and fails over automatically. --next-hop-instance expects a VM name, --next-hop-gateway only accepts the default internet gateway, and --next-hop-vpn-tunnel expects a Cloud VPN tunnel.

question: Private VMs in prod-vpc suddenly lost outbound internet access through Cloud NAT. The NAT gateway and Cloud Router are unchanged, and egress firewall rules allow the traffic. An audit log shows someone deleted the route for 0.0.0.0/0. Which command restores outbound access?
options: gcloud compute routers update rtr-1 --region=us-central1 --advertisement-mode=CUSTOM --set-advertisement-ranges=0.0.0.0/0
gcloud compute routers nats update nat-1 --router=rtr-1 --region=us-central1 --auto-allocate-nat-external-ips --nat-all-subnet-ip-ranges
gcloud compute routes create default-egress --network=prod-vpc --destination-range=0.0.0.0/0 --next-hop-gateway=default-internet-gateway
gcloud compute routes create default-egress --network=prod-vpc --destination-range=0.0.0.0/0 --next-hop-instance=nat-gateway-vm
explanation: Cloud NAT is not a route next hop; Public NAT still needs a route to 0.0.0.0/0 whose next hop is the default internet gateway, so recreating that route restores egress. Changing NAT IP allocation does not replace the missing route, a NAT instance VM is a different design, and Cloud Router advertisements affect BGP peers rather than the VPC's own routing.

question: A VM behind Cloud NAT opens thousands of concurrent connections to one external API. Cloud NAT logs for the VM show dropped connections with the reason OUT_OF_RESOURCES. The gateway uses static port allocation with default settings. Which change most directly addresses the drops?
options: gcloud compute routers nats update nat-1 --router=rtr-1 --region=us-east1 --enable-logging --log-filter=ALL
gcloud compute routers nats update nat-1 --router=rtr-1 --region=us-east1 --log-filter=ERRORS_ONLY
gcloud compute routers nats update nat-1 --router=rtr-1 --region=us-east1 --nat-primary-subnet-ip-ranges
gcloud compute routers nats update nat-1 --router=rtr-1 --region=us-east1 --min-ports-per-vm=4096
explanation: OUT_OF_RESOURCES means the VM ran out of NAT source ports, and with static allocation each VM gets 64 ports by default, so raising the minimum ports per VM gives it more concurrent connections; adding NAT IPs or enabling dynamic port allocation are other options. Logging and log filter changes only change what is recorded, and changing which subnet ranges are NATed does not add ports.

question: A partner only accepts traffic from two known source IPs. Private VMs in us-west1 reach the partner through the Cloud NAT gateway nat-west, which currently allocates IPs automatically. You reserved the regional static external IPs nat-ip-1 and nat-ip-2. What should you do?
options: Assign nat-ip-1 and nat-ip-2 as external IPs on two of the VMs and route the other VMs' traffic through those two VMs as proxies
Run gcloud compute routers nats update nat-west --router=rtr-west --region=us-west1 --auto-allocate-nat-external-ips
Run gcloud compute routers update rtr-west --region=us-west1 --set-advertisement-ranges=nat-ip-1,nat-ip-2
Run gcloud compute routers nats update nat-west --router=rtr-west --region=us-west1 --nat-external-ip-pool=nat-ip-1,nat-ip-2
explanation: Switching the gateway to manual allocation with --nat-external-ip-pool makes all NAT traffic use the reserved static addresses, which the partner can allowlist. Automatic allocation can add or change IPs, adding external IPs to VMs breaks the private design and needs extra routing, and Cloud Router advertisements do not choose NAT source addresses.

question: All VMs in a subnet send traffic to a partner through Cloud NAT, and the partner allowlists the NAT IP. One VM, report-1, is rejected by the partner, which sees a different source IP for it. NAT and firewall settings are the same for every VM. What is the most likely cause?
options: report-1 runs a container-optimized image, and Cloud NAT does not translate traffic generated inside containers
report-1 has an external IP on its network interface, so its traffic leaves through that IP instead of Cloud NAT
report-1 is in a different zone, and Cloud NAT only translates traffic from VMs in the zone of its Cloud Router
Cloud NAT gives each VM a random source IP from Google's pool, so report-1 needs its own NAT gateway instance
explanation: Cloud NAT does not apply to a network interface that has its own external IP, so that VM's traffic uses its external address and the partner sees a different source. Removing the external IP makes the VM use the NAT gateway. NAT IPs come from the gateway's configured addresses, and Cloud NAT is regional rather than zonal and does not depend on the guest image.

question: VMs in the VPC prod-vpc must resolve names such as db.corp.internal, and these names must not be resolvable from the internet. Which command creates the zone that holds these records?
options: gcloud dns managed-zones create corp-internal --dns-name=corp.internal. --target-network=prod-vpc --visibility=private --description=Internal
gcloud dns managed-zones create corp-internal --dns-name=corp.internal. --visibility=public --networks=prod-vpc --description=Internal
gcloud dns managed-zones create corp-internal --dns-name=corp.internal. --visibility=private --networks=prod-vpc --description=Internal
gcloud dns managed-zones create corp-internal --dns-name=corp.internal. --visibility=private --forwarding-targets=10.0.0.2 --description=Internal
explanation: A private managed zone created with --visibility=private and --networks is only visible to the listed VPC networks, so the records resolve inside prod-vpc and not on the internet. The default public visibility publishes the zone to the internet. Forwarding targets send queries to other name servers instead of hosting records, and --target-network creates a peering zone.

question: VMs in prod-vpc must resolve names under onprem.example.com. Those names are served only by on-premises DNS servers at 192.168.10.53 and 192.168.10.54, which are reachable over Cloud VPN. What should you configure in Cloud DNS?
options: A private forwarding zone for onprem.example.com. visible to prod-vpc, with --forwarding-targets=192.168.10.53,192.168.10.54
A public zone for onprem.example.com. with NS records that point at 192.168.10.53 and 192.168.10.54 over the VPN tunnel
A private zone for onprem.example.com. visible to prod-vpc, with A records copied by hand from the on-premises servers
A private peering zone for onprem.example.com. with --target-network set to the VPN tunnel that connects to the data center
explanation: A private forwarding zone sends queries for the domain from the authorized VPC to the target name servers, and RFC 1918 targets are reached through the VPC and its VPN. A public zone is not used for private hybrid resolution, a peering zone targets another VPC network rather than a tunnel, and copying records by hand quickly goes stale.

question: In a custom-mode VPC, you want to record connection attempts that are blocked because no firewall rule allows them, so you can audit them. You find that you cannot enable logging on the implied deny ingress rule. What should you do?
options: Create an ingress allow rule for all sources at priority 65535 with --enable-logging, which records traffic before denial
Edit the implied deny ingress rule to priority 65534 and enable logging on it with gcloud compute firewall-rules update
Create an ingress deny rule for all sources at priority 65534 with --enable-logging, so it matches traffic before the implied deny
Enable VPC Flow Logs on every subnet, because flow logs record which firewall rule denied each packet that was dropped
explanation: Firewall rules logging is not supported for the implied deny ingress and implied allow egress rules, so you add an explicit low-priority deny rule with logging enabled that catches the same traffic just before the implied rule. Implied rules cannot be edited, an allow rule at 65535 would permit the traffic, and VPC Flow Logs do not report which firewall rule denied a connection.

question: A global network firewall policy associated with app-vpc has an ingress allow rule for TCP 443 from the load balancer health-check ranges. Health checks still fail. app-vpc also has a VPC firewall rule that denies all ingress TCP 443 at priority 1000. The network uses the default enforcement order. Why does the traffic fail?
options: Global network firewall policy rules can only target network tags, and the backend VMs do not carry the tag the rule expects
The policy rule and the VPC rule share priority 1000, and when priorities tie across both types, the deny action always takes precedence
Global network firewall policies only apply to egress traffic, so ingress for health checks is controlled only by VPC firewall rules
VPC firewall rules are evaluated before the global network firewall policy by default, so the VPC deny matches and evaluation stops
explanation: With the default AFTER_CLASSIC_FIREWALL order, Google Cloud evaluates hierarchical policies, then VPC firewall rules, then global network firewall policies, and a matching allow or deny ends evaluation. The VPC deny matches first, so the policy's allow is never reached; fix the VPC rule or change the enforcement order. Priorities are not compared across these steps, policies apply to ingress, and policy rules target secure tags or service accounts.

question: The VM web-1 in us-central1-a cannot connect to a PostgreSQL server at 10.30.0.5 on TCP 5432. You want Google Cloud to analyze the configured routes and firewall rules along the path and report where packets would be dropped. Which command should you run?
options: gcloud compute firewall-rules list --filter=network=prod-vpc --format=json --sort-by=priority, then compare each ingress and egress rule by hand with the network tags and service account of web-1
gcloud compute ssh web-1 --zone=us-central1-a --command='nc -vz 10.30.0.5 5432', then read the exit code of the command to work out which hop in the path dropped the packets
gcloud compute routes list --filter=network=prod-vpc --format=json --sort-by=priority, then trace by hand which route and next hop match 10.30.0.5 from the subnet of web-1

gcloud network-management connectivity-tests create web-to-db --source-instance=projects/prj/zones/us-central1-a/instances/web-1 --destination-ip-address=10.30.0.5 --destination-port=5432 --protocol=TCP
explanation: Connectivity Tests in Network Intelligence Center model the configured path between a source and a destination, check routes and firewall rules, and report the step where packets would be dropped. Listing rules or routes only gives raw configuration to analyze by hand, and a netcat probe shows that the connection fails but not which configuration blocks it.

question: Your VPC has accumulated hundreds of firewall rules over several years. You want to find allow rules that can never match traffic because higher-priority rules already cover all of their attributes, so that you can remove them safely. Which tool should you use?
options: Cloud Asset Inventory export of firewall rules, compared rule by rule by hand
Firewall Insights in Network Intelligence Center, which reports shadowed rules
VPC Flow Logs on every subnet, queried in Log Analytics for each rule name
Connectivity Tests in Network Intelligence Center, run once for every rule
explanation: Firewall Insights analyzes firewall rule configuration and usage and identifies shadowed rules, which are fully covered by other rules with higher priority and never apply. Connectivity Tests check one path at a time, flow logs record traffic rather than rule relationships, and an asset export would still need manual analysis.

question: The subnet batch-subnet uses 10.60.0.0/20, but only about 100 addresses are in use, and the network team wants to give part of that space to another subnet by changing it to 10.60.0.0/24. What should you do?
options: Run gcloud compute networks subnets expand-ip-range batch-subnet with --prefix-length=24 to reduce the range in place while VMs keep running
Add 10.60.0.0/24 as a secondary range on batch-subnet and remove the primary range, which converts the secondary range into the primary one
Create a new subnet with the smaller range and migrate workloads to it, because a primary range cannot be shrunk
Run gcloud compute networks subnets update batch-subnet with --range=10.60.0.0/24, which reclaims unused addresses and keeps the VMs' IPs
explanation: You can expand a subnet's primary IPv4 range, but you cannot shrink it or undo an expansion, so the only way to use a smaller range is to build a new subnet and move the workloads. expand-ip-range only accepts a shorter prefix length, the update command has no option to shrink the primary range, and a primary range cannot be removed or replaced by a secondary range.

question: Your team keeps Cloud Monitoring alerting policies as JSON files in a Git repository. A pipeline must create the policy defined in cpu-high.json in the project ops-prod. Which command should the pipeline run?
options: gcloud monitoring policies create --policy-from-file=cpu-high.json --project=ops-prod
gcloud monitoring alerts create --config-from-file=cpu-high.json --project=ops-prod
gcloud logging metrics create cpu-high --config-from-file=cpu-high.json --project=ops-prod
gcloud monitoring dashboards create --config-from-file=cpu-high.json --project=ops-prod
explanation: Alerting policies are created with gcloud monitoring policies create, and the --policy-from-file flag reads a JSON or YAML AlertPolicy definition. There is no monitoring alerts command group, logging metrics create builds log-based metrics, and dashboards create builds dashboards rather than alerting policies.

question: A custom exporter on a Compute Engine VM writes a business metric to Cloud Monitoring every minute. If the exporter process crashes, the metric simply stops receiving data and nobody notices. You want to be notified when no data has arrived for 30 minutes. What should you configure?
options: A forecast condition that predicts when the metric value will fall to zero
A metric-absence condition on the custom metric with a 30-minute duration
An uptime check against the VM's external IP address on TCP port 22
A log-based alerting policy that matches ERROR entries from the exporter
explanation: A metric-absence condition fires when a time series stops receiving data for the configured duration, which is exactly the crashed-exporter case. A forecast condition predicts future values of data that is still arriving, an SSH uptime check only proves the VM is reachable, and a crashed process may never write an ERROR log entry.

question: An engineer who used Monitoring Query Language (MQL) at a previous company is about to write several new alerting policy conditions in the Google Cloud console. Which query language does Google now recommend for new charts and alerting conditions in Cloud Monitoring?
options: MQL, because it is still the default editor for new console alerting policies
GoogleSQL run in Log Analytics and attached to the alerting policy as a condition
PromQL, which Cloud Monitoring supports in the code editor for charts and alerts
The Logging query language, applied through a log-based metric for each condition
explanation: Google no longer recommends MQL; support ended in July 2025 and MQL is no longer offered in the console for new charts and alerting policies, with PromQL (or the query builder) recommended instead. Log Analytics SQL is for querying logs, and the Logging query language selects log entries rather than defining metric conditions.

question: Your incident-management tool runs in your on-premises data center and is reachable from Google Cloud only through Cloud VPN on a private IP address. Cloud Monitoring webhook notifications to that tool never arrive. You want alert notifications delivered to the tool reliably. What should you do?
options: Add basic authentication to the webhook channel so Monitoring can reach the private address
Create an SMS notification channel that targets the tool's on-premises SMS gateway number
Add a firewall rule that allows the uptime-check source IP addresses to reach the tool
Use a Pub/Sub notification channel and have the tool pull messages from a subscription
explanation: Monitoring webhooks support only public endpoints, so for a private endpoint Google recommends a Pub/Sub notification channel with a subscription that the tool consumes. Authentication does not make a private address reachable, SMS is not a reliable integration path, and uptime-check IPs are unrelated to notification delivery.

question: You created a public HTTPS uptime check for a web server on a Compute Engine VM. A VPC firewall rule allows ingress on port 443 only from an approved list of source addresses, and the uptime check reports failures from every region. You need the addresses to add to the allow list. Which command provides them?
options: gcloud compute addresses list --filter=purpose=UPTIME_CHECK
gcloud monitoring uptime list-ips
gcloud monitoring uptime list-configs
gcloud compute firewall-rules create allow-uptime --source-ranges=35.199.192.0/19
explanation: The gcloud monitoring uptime list-ips command lists the IP addresses used by uptime-check servers so you can allow them through firewalls. list-configs lists your uptime check definitions, reserved addresses are unrelated, and 35.199.192.0/19 is the source range used by private uptime checks, not public ones.

question: An internal HTTP API runs behind an internal Application Load Balancer and has no public IP address. You want Cloud Monitoring to probe the API endpoint regularly and alert when it stops responding. What should you configure?
options: A public uptime check against an ephemeral external IP address added to the load balancer
A Cloud NAT gateway so that uptime-check servers can reach the backends over the internet
A private uptime check that targets a Service Directory service with the ILB's IP and port
A metric-absence alert on the Ops Agent heartbeat metric from each backend virtual machine
explanation: Private uptime checks probe internal endpoints through a Service Directory service whose endpoint holds the internal IP address and port, with ingress allowed from 35.199.192.0/19. Exposing the load balancer publicly defeats the design, Cloud NAT is outbound only, and an agent heartbeat does not test whether the API responds.

question: You exported a custom Cloud Monitoring dashboard to the file ops-dash.json and want to recreate it in a new project named web-staging as part of an automated environment build. Which command should you use?
options: gcloud monitoring dashboards import --source=ops-dash.json --project=web-staging
gcloud monitoring policies create --policy-from-file=ops-dash.json --project=web-staging
gcloud logging views create ops-dash --config-from-file=ops-dash.json --project=web-staging
gcloud monitoring dashboards create --config-from-file=ops-dash.json --project=web-staging
explanation: gcloud monitoring dashboards create accepts a JSON or YAML dashboard definition through --config-from-file. There is no dashboards import command, policies create builds alerting policies, and logging views control access to log buckets rather than defining dashboards.

question: A central operations team must view CPU, memory, and request metrics from 40 application projects in shared dashboards and manage alerting policies for all of them from one place. What should you set up?
options: A dedicated scoping project whose metrics scope includes the 40 projects as monitored projects
An aggregated log sink on the parent folder that routes all logs to a central log bucket
A Shared VPC host project with all 40 application projects attached to it as service projects
A daily export of each project's metrics to BigQuery, with dashboards built in Looker Studio
explanation: A metrics scope lets a scoping project chart and alert on time-series data from many monitored projects, and Google recommends a dedicated scoping project for this. An aggregated sink centralizes logs, not metrics, Shared VPC is a networking construct, and a BigQuery export adds work and is not near real time.

question: An application writes a custom metric to the Cloud Monitoring API once per second for a single time series. Many writes are rejected with errors even though the project's API quota is far from exhausted. What should you change?
options: Rename the metric with the logging.googleapis.com/user/ prefix to get a higher write limit
Aggregate locally and write no more than one point every 5 seconds to each time series
Request an increase to the per-minute time series write quota for the Monitoring API
Change the metric kind from GAUGE to CUMULATIVE so that one-second writes are accepted
explanation: Cloud Monitoring limits writes to a single time series to one point every 5 seconds, so the application should aggregate and write less often. That limit is per time series, so a quota increase does not help, the logging.googleapis.com/user/ prefix belongs to log-based metrics, and changing the metric kind does not change the write rate limit.

question: A Cloud Run service writes a structured log entry for every page render with the field jsonPayload.render_ms. You need a chart of the 95th percentile render time and an alert when it exceeds 800 ms. What should you create?
options: A counter log-based metric whose filter matches entries where render_ms is greater than 800
A counter log-based metric with a label that extracts render_ms from each matching entry
A log-based alerting policy whose query matches entries where render_ms is greater than 800
A distribution log-based metric whose value extractor reads the jsonPayload.render_ms field
explanation: A distribution log-based metric extracts a numeric value from each entry into histogram buckets, so you can chart and alert on percentiles. A counter only counts matching entries, a label holding raw latency values creates high cardinality without percentiles, and a log-based alert fires on individual entries rather than on a percentile.

question: You wrote checkout-latency.yaml, which defines a log filter, a valueExtractor that uses REGEXP_EXTRACT, bucketOptions, and a DISTRIBUTION value type. Which command creates the log-based metric from this file?
options: gcloud logging metrics create checkout_latency --config-from-file=checkout-latency.yaml
gcloud logging metrics create checkout_latency --log-filter=checkout --metric-kind=distribution
gcloud monitoring policies create --policy-from-file=checkout-latency.yaml --project=shop-prod
gcloud logging sinks create checkout_latency monitoring.googleapis.com --log-filter=checkout
explanation: Distribution log-based metrics need a value extractor and bucket options, which gcloud logging metrics create reads from a LogMetric definition passed with --config-from-file. There is no --metric-kind flag for log-based metrics, policies create builds alerting policies, and Cloud Monitoring is not a sink destination.

question: You added an exclusion filter to the _Default sink so that load balancer health-check entries are no longer stored. A user-defined counter log-based metric on those health-check entries still increases, but a log-based alerting policy with the same query never fires. What explains this?
options: Exclusion filters apply only to log-based alerts, and metrics read the _Required bucket
User-defined log-based metrics evaluate excluded logs, but log-based alerts evaluate only included logs
The log-based alert is waiting for its default notification rate limit of seven days to expire
Log-based alerting policies only evaluate audit logs, while metrics evaluate all log types
explanation: By default, user-defined log-based metrics are calculated from both included and excluded logs, whereas log-based alerting policies do not evaluate excluded logs. Health-check entries are not written to the _Required bucket, seven days is the default auto-close duration rather than a rate limit, and log-based alerts work on any log type.

question: The security team wants a notification for each new service account key creation in a production project. The notification must name the principal that created the key, and the team wants at most one notification every 5 minutes. What should you do?
options: Create a counter log-based metric and a metric-threshold alert that fires above zero
Configure Error Reporting notifications for errors reported by the IAM API in the project
Create a log-based alerting policy from a Logs Explorer query with a 5-minute rate limit
Create a Pub/Sub sink for the audit entries and subscribe the security team's mailing list
explanation: A log-based alerting policy triggers on individual matching entries, includes details of the entry, and supports a notification rate limit such as 5 minutes. A counter metric loses the per-entry details, Error Reporting groups application exceptions rather than audit events, and Pub/Sub cannot deliver messages directly to an email list.

question: You have planned maintenance on Saturday from 01:00 to 03:00 UTC. Three alerting policies will fire during the work, and you want their notifications suppressed for exactly that window without anyone having to re-enable anything afterward. What should you do?
options: Disable the three policies with gcloud monitoring policies update before the work starts
Disable the notification channels used by the policies, then re-enable them at 03:00
Disable the _Default sink so that no new log entries reach the alerting policies
Create a snooze with gcloud monitoring snoozes create that lists the three policies
explanation: A snooze suppresses alerts and notifications from selected alerting policies between a start and end time, then ends on its own. Disabling policies or channels needs a manual step afterward and can be forgotten, and disabling the _Default sink stops log storage without affecting metric-based policies.

question: Project app-prod must send its Cloud Run logs to the log bucket central-bucket in us-central1, which belongs to the project log-hub. Which command creates the sink in app-prod?
options: gcloud logging sinks create to-hub logging.googleapis.com/projects/log-hub/locations/us-central1/buckets/central-bucket --log-filter='resource.type="cloud_run_revision"'
gcloud logging sinks create to-hub logging.googleapis.com/projects/log-hub/buckets/central-bucket --log-filter='resource.type="cloud_run_revision"'
gcloud logging sinks create to-hub storage.googleapis.com/log-hub/central-bucket --log-filter='resource.type="cloud_run_revision"'
gcloud logging buckets create to-hub --location=us-central1 --project=log-hub --log-filter='resource.type="cloud_run_revision"'
explanation: A log bucket destination uses the format logging.googleapis.com/projects/PROJECT/locations/LOCATION/buckets/BUCKET, so the location segment is required. The storage.googleapis.com form targets a Cloud Storage bucket, and buckets create makes a bucket but does not route any logs to it.

question: You created a sink in project web-prod that routes request logs to a BigQuery dataset in project analytics-hub. Hours later, no tables have appeared in the dataset, and the sink shows a writer identity service account. What should you do?
options: Grant your own user account the BigQuery Admin role on the analytics-hub project
Grant the sink's writer identity the BigQuery Data Editor role on the destination
Enable Data Access audit logs for BigQuery in both of the projects involved
Grant the Compute Engine default service account BigQuery Data Editor on the dataset
explanation: A sink writes as its writer identity, and for a BigQuery destination in another project that identity needs BigQuery Data Editor on the dataset or its project. Your own permissions and the Compute Engine default service account are not used by the sink, and Data Access audit logs have nothing to do with sink delivery.

question: Twenty minutes ago you created a sink that routes Compute Engine logs to a Cloud Storage bucket. The writer identity has the correct role, but the bucket is still empty although new matching entries appear in Logs Explorer. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The bucket must use uniform bucket-level access before sinks can write objects to it
The sink is first back-filling older entries and will write new entries only afterward
Cloud Storage sinks write in hourly batches, and a new sink can take hours to start
Data Access audit logs must be enabled for Cloud Storage before sinks can write to it
explanation: Log sinks to Cloud Storage are processed hourly, and a new Cloud Storage sink can take several hours to begin routing. Sinks never route entries received before they were created, and neither uniform bucket-level access nor Data Access audit logs is a prerequisite for a sink.

question: Your security operations center runs a SIEM in an on-premises data center and needs Google Cloud audit logs delivered in near real time. The SIEM vendor supports consuming messages from Google Cloud. What should you do?
options: Create a sink whose destination is the SIEM's syslog URL on the on-premises network
Route the logs to a Cloud Storage bucket and have the SIEM download the hourly object files
Create a linked BigQuery dataset and have the SIEM poll it with scheduled queries
Route the logs to a Pub/Sub topic and have the SIEM, or a Dataflow job, subscribe to it
explanation: Pub/Sub is the sink destination designed for streaming logs to third-party and on-premises systems, either by a subscriber or a Dataflow pipeline. Sinks cannot target arbitrary URLs, Cloud Storage sinks write hourly batches, and polling BigQuery adds delay and query cost.

question: All projects in the folder retail must send their logs to a central log bucket. To avoid paying twice, the logs must not also be stored in each project's _Default bucket, though each project's _Required bucket must keep working. Projects created later must be covered automatically. What should you do?
options: Create a folder sink with --include-children and --intercept-children to the central bucket
Create a folder sink with --include-children only, which stops the projects' own sinks
Create a sink in every project to the central bucket and disable each project's _Default sink
Add an exclusion filter to the folder's _Default sink that matches all entries from child projects
explanation: An intercepting aggregated sink routes matching entries from child resources to its destination and stops them from reaching the children's sinks, except the _Required sink, and it covers new projects. A non-intercepting sink leaves project sinks active, per-project sinks do not cover future projects automatically, and the folder's _Default sink handles only folder-level logs.

question: HTTP load balancer request logs with status 200 make up most of your logging bill. You want to keep roughly 10% of those entries for trend analysis and drop the rest, while keeping every non-200 entry. Which exclusion filter should you add to the _Default sink?
options: resource.type="http_load_balancer" AND httpRequest.status=200 AND sample(insertId, 0.1)
resource.type="http_load_balancer" AND httpRequest.status=200 AND sample(insertId, 0.9)
resource.type="http_load_balancer" AND httpRequest.status!=200 AND sample(insertId, 0.9)
resource.type="http_load_balancer" AND sample(insertId, 0.1) AND severity>=DEFAULT
explanation: An exclusion filter drops what it matches, and sample(insertId, 0.9) matches about 90% of entries, so about 10% of the status-200 entries are kept. Using 0.1 would drop only 10% of them, filtering on status!=200 would drop the entries you must keep, and the last filter samples every status code.

question: Health-check requests from a Cloud Run service generate millions of INFO entries per day that nobody uses. You want to stop storing them in the project while every other log keeps flowing as before. Which command should you run?
options: gcloud logging sinks update _Required --add-exclusion=name=drop-hc,filter='httpRequest.requestUrl:"/healthz"'
gcloud logging buckets update _Default --location=global --add-exclusion=name=drop-hc,filter='httpRequest.requestUrl:"/healthz"'
gcloud logging sinks update _Default --add-exclusion=name=drop-hc,filter='httpRequest.requestUrl:"/healthz"'
gcloud logging metrics create drop-hc --log-filter='httpRequest.requestUrl:"/healthz"' --exclude
explanation: Exclusions belong to sinks, so adding one to the _Default sink with --add-exclusion stops matching entries from being stored in the _Default bucket. The _Required sink cannot be modified, log buckets do not hold exclusion filters, and log-based metrics count entries rather than dropping them.

question: An auditor requires you to keep Admin Activity audit logs for seven years. Your attempt to change the retention of the _Required log bucket fails. What should you do?
options: Lock the _Required bucket with gcloud logging buckets update so its retention is extended
Open a support case to raise the _Required bucket's retention from 400 days to seven years
Change the organization's default resource settings so new _Required buckets keep seven years
Route the Admin Activity logs to a user-defined log bucket that has 2,555-day retention
explanation: The _Required bucket keeps its logs for 400 days, and that retention cannot be changed, so longer retention needs a sink to a user-defined bucket, whose retention can be set from 1 to 3,650 days. Locking does not extend retention, and neither support nor default settings can change the _Required bucket.

question: Logs in your project's _Default bucket currently expire after the default period. Your team wants them kept for 90 days. Which command should you run?
options: gcloud logging buckets update _Default --location=global --retention-days=90
gcloud logging sinks update _Default --retention-days=90 --location=global
gcloud logging buckets update _Required --location=global --retention-days=90
gcloud logging buckets update _Default --location=global --retention-period=90d
explanation: Retention is a property of the log bucket and is set with gcloud logging buckets update and --retention-days. Sinks do not hold retention settings, the _Required bucket's retention cannot be changed, and --retention-period is a Cloud Storage flag rather than a Cloud Logging one.

question: A regulator requires that nobody, including project owners, can shorten the retention period of your audit-logs log bucket or delete it before its logs expire. What should you do after setting the retention period?
options: Set a Cloud Storage retention policy and bucket lock on the log bucket with gcloud storage
Lock the bucket with gcloud logging buckets update audit-logs --location=us-east1 --locked
Remove the Logging Admin role from every project owner on the project that holds the bucket
Create a log view on the bucket and grant the auditors only the Logs View Accessor role
explanation: Locking a log bucket with --locked is irreversible and prevents changes to its retention policy and deletion of the bucket until entries pass retention. Log buckets are not Cloud Storage buckets, removing roles can be undone by any owner, and log views only control who can read entries.

question: Analysts want to query an existing user-defined log bucket named app-logs in us-central1 with SQL on the Log Analytics page, but the bucket has not been upgraded. Which command should you run first?
options: gcloud logging links create app_logs_link --bucket=app-logs --location=us-central1
bq mk --dataset --location=us-central1 app_logs and grant the analysts Data Viewer
gcloud logging buckets update app-logs --location=us-central1 --enable-analytics --async
gcloud logging views create analysts --bucket=app-logs --location=us-central1
explanation: Log Analytics requires the bucket to be upgraded with --enable-analytics, an irreversible operation that Google suggests running with --async. A linked BigQuery dataset can be created only after the upgrade, a plain BigQuery dataset holds no logs, and a log view controls access but does not enable SQL.

question: Logs in an upgraded log bucket must be joined with a customer table in BigQuery by using existing BigQuery tools. You want to avoid a second copy of the logs and the ingestion work of a separate export. What should you do?
options: Create a BigQuery sink that streams the same logs into a dataset next to the customer table
Route the logs to Cloud Storage and define a BigQuery external table over the exported files
Create a log view on the bucket and grant the analysts the Logs View Accessor role on it
Create a linked BigQuery dataset for the bucket with gcloud logging links create
explanation: A linked dataset exposes the logs in an upgraded log bucket to BigQuery without copying them, so they can be joined with other BigQuery tables. A BigQuery or Cloud Storage sink creates a second copy and more pipeline work, and a log view grants read access in Logging but does not make the logs queryable from BigQuery.

question: In a new project, developers run BigQuery queries and read objects from a Cloud Storage bucket. Nobody has changed the audit log configuration. Which Data Access audit log entries will you find in Cloud Logging?
options: Entries for the BigQuery queries only
Entries for both the queries and the object reads
No Data Access entries for either service
Entries for the Cloud Storage object reads only
explanation: Data Access audit logs are disabled by default for every service except BigQuery, whose Data Access logs are written by default. Cloud Storage object reads are logged only after you enable Data Access logs for Cloud Storage.

question: You enabled DATA_READ audit logs for Cloud Storage. A backup service account now produces millions of read entries each day, and you want to stop recording only that account's reads while keeping reads by everyone else. How should you change the IAM policy's audit configuration?
options: Remove DATA_READ from the storage.googleapis.com audit configuration and keep only DATA_WRITE
Add the backup service account to exemptedMembers for DATA_READ on storage.googleapis.com
Add an exclusion filter for the backup service account's principal email to the _Required sink
Revoke the backup service account's Logs Writer role so its reads stop producing log entries
explanation: The auditConfigs section of an IAM policy lets you list principals in exemptedMembers for a log type, so their data access is not recorded while other principals' is. Removing DATA_READ stops logging reads by everyone, the _Required sink cannot take exclusion filters, and audit logs are written by Google services regardless of the caller's Logging roles.

question: Requests from a developer workstation to BigQuery in the project sec-prod are being blocked by a VPC Service Controls perimeter. You want to see the denied requests and the reason. Which Logs Explorer query should you use?
options: logName="projects/sec-prod/logs/cloudaudit.googleapis.com%2Fdata_access"
logName="projects/sec-prod/logs/compute.googleapis.com%2Ffirewall"
logName="projects/sec-prod/logs/cloudaudit.googleapis.com%2Fpolicy"
logName="projects/sec-prod/logs/cloudaudit.googleapis.com%2Fsystem_event"
explanation: Requests denied by a VPC Service Controls policy are recorded in Policy Denied audit logs, whose log name ends in cloudaudit.googleapis.com%2Fpolicy and which are generated by default. Data Access logs record permitted data operations, firewall logs record VPC firewall rule matches, and System Event logs record actions taken by Google systems.

question: A production VM was deleted yesterday. You found the Admin Activity audit entry for the delete call and need the field that identifies who made the request. Which field should you read?
options: protoPayload.requestMetadata.callerIp
resource.labels.instance_id
protoPayload.serviceName
protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail
explanation: In an audit log entry, the authenticationInfo field records the caller, and principalEmail holds the user or service account that made the request. callerIp gives only the source address, resource.labels.instance_id identifies the VM, and serviceName identifies the API, such as compute.googleapis.com.

question: For a network investigation, you need VPC Flow Logs on the subnet web-subnet in us-east1. To limit cost, you want only 25% of flows sampled and records aggregated over 1-minute intervals. Which command should you run?
options: gcloud compute networks subnets update web-subnet --region=us-east1 --enable-flow-logs --logging-flow-sampling=0.25 --logging-aggregation-interval=interval-1-min
gcloud compute networks update web-subnet --region=us-east1 --enable-flow-logs --logging-flow-sampling=25 --logging-aggregation-interval=interval-1-min
gcloud compute firewall-rules update web-subnet --enable-logging --logging-flow-sampling=0.25 --logging-aggregation-interval=interval-1-min
gcloud logging sinks create web-subnet --region=us-east1 --enable-flow-logs --logging-flow-sampling=0.25 --logging-aggregation-interval=1m
explanation: With the Compute Engine API, flow logs are enabled per subnet with gcloud compute networks subnets update and --enable-flow-logs, where sampling is a fraction from 0 to 1 and interval-1-min is a valid aggregation value. Networks update does not configure subnets, firewall rule logging is a separate feature, and sinks route logs rather than generate them.

question: A VPC network has dozens of subnets plus several Cloud VPN tunnels and VLAN attachments. You want flow logs for all of them by using a single configuration rather than one setting per subnet. What should you do?
options: Enable Firewall Rules Logging on every firewall rule in the network with --enable-logging
Create a VPC Flow Logs configuration for the whole network with the Network Management API
Create an aggregated log sink with --include-children that selects the vpc_flows log name
Create a Packet Mirroring policy for the network that sends traffic to a collector
explanation: The Network Management API supports VPC Flow Logs configurations scoped to an entire VPC network, covering its subnets, VLAN attachments, and Cloud VPN tunnels with gcloud network-management vpc-flow-logs-configs create. Firewall logging records rule matches, sinks only route logs that already exist, and Packet Mirroring copies full packets at much higher cost.

question: You need to log every inbound connection attempt that is blocked in a custom-mode VPC network. The network currently has a few allow rules and relies on the implied deny ingress rule for everything else. What should you do?
options: Enable logging on the implied deny ingress rule with gcloud compute firewall-rules update
Enable Data Access audit logs for compute.googleapis.com in the project's IAM policy
Enable logging on the existing allow rules so that rejected connections are recorded too
Create an ingress deny rule for 0.0.0.0/0 at priority 65534 with logging enabled
explanation: Firewall Rules Logging cannot be enabled for the implied rules, so you add an explicit low-priority deny rule with logging that matches traffic the allow rules do not. Logging on allow rules records only allowed connections, and Data Access audit logs record API calls rather than network traffic.

question: A request to your storefront passes through four Cloud Run services before it returns. Some requests take eight seconds, and you need to find which service-to-service call adds the delay for a specific slow request. Which tool should you use?
options: Cloud Trace, with the services instrumented by OpenTelemetry to propagate trace context
Cloud Profiler, with an agent added to each service to capture CPU and heap profiles
Error Reporting, with the slow requests grouped by the Cloud Run service that returned them
Cloud Debugger, with snapshots taken in each service while the slow request runs
explanation: Cloud Trace records distributed traces, so you can see the latency of each span across the services for a single request. Profiler shows aggregate resource use by function rather than per-request latency, Error Reporting groups exceptions, and Cloud Debugger has been retired.

question: A Java service on GKE uses much more CPU in production than in testing, and you cannot reproduce the load. You want continuous, low-overhead data from production that shows which methods consume CPU and allocate memory. What should you use?
options: Cloud Trace, with the sampling rate raised to record every request in production
Cloud Profiler, by adding the Java profiling agent to the service's container image
Query Insights, enabled on the service's database to show the most expensive queries
Cloud Debugger, by setting logpoints in the methods you suspect are consuming CPU
explanation: Cloud Profiler continuously samples CPU and heap use in production with low overhead and shows the results by function in flame graphs. Trace measures request latency rather than CPU by method, Query Insights covers database queries, and Cloud Debugger is a retired product.

question: Your application logs thousands of known errors each day. The on-call team wants a notification only when a new kind of exception appears or when an error group they marked Resolved occurs again. What should you configure?
options: A log-based alerting policy that matches every entry with severity greater than or equal to ERROR
A metric-threshold alert on the log entry count metric filtered to ERROR severity entries
Error Reporting notifications, sent to the team's notification channel for the project
An uptime check against the application with an alerting policy on failed checks
explanation: Error Reporting sends notifications when an error cannot be grouped with existing errors and when an error recurs in a group marked Resolved, which matches the requirement. A log-based alert or count threshold fires on known errors too, and an uptime check tests availability rather than exception types.

question: A Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL Enterprise Plus instance has Query insights enabled. Several frequent queries perform full table scans, and you want suggestions of which indexes to create along with their estimated impact. Where should you look?
options: The Active Assist idle resource recommendations for the Cloud SQL instance
The Cloud Profiler flame graph for the application that runs the queries
The System Event audit logs written for the Cloud SQL instance's maintenance
The index advisor recommendations shown in the Query insights dashboard
explanation: Index advisor analyzes queries and recommends CREATE INDEX statements with their expected performance impact, shown in the Query insights dashboard for Enterprise Plus instances. Idle resource recommendations target unused resources, Profiler analyzes application code, and System Event logs record Google-initiated actions.

question: Your team wants a Slack message whenever Google Cloud publishes or updates an incident that affects the products and regions used by your projects. What should you do?
options: Enable the Service Health API and create an alerting policy from a Service Health alert template
Subscribe the Slack channel to the public Google Cloud Service Health status page RSS feed
Create uptime checks against the Google API endpoints in each region your projects use
Configure Error Reporting notifications for errors returned by Google Cloud APIs
explanation: Personalized Service Health shows incidents relevant to your projects and provides alert templates that create Cloud Monitoring alerting policies with notification channels such as Slack, after the Service Health API is enabled. The public status feed is not personalized, uptime checks test only reachability, and Error Reporting groups your application's own exceptions.

question: You need to install the Ops Agent on a single Debian Compute Engine VM to collect guest OS metrics and logs. After connecting over SSH and downloading Google's repository script, which command installs the agent?
options: sudo bash install-logging-agent.sh --structured
sudo bash add-google-cloud-ops-agent-repo.sh --also-install
sudo apt-get install stackdriver-agent google-fluentd
sudo bash add-monitoring-agent-repo.sh --also-install
explanation: The add-google-cloud-ops-agent-repo.sh script adds the package repository, and the --also-install flag installs the Ops Agent. The install-logging-agent.sh, stackdriver-agent, google-fluentd, and add-monitoring-agent-repo.sh options all belong to the legacy Logging and Monitoring agents that the Ops Agent replaces.

question: The Ops Agent runs on a Linux VM and already sends syslog entries. An application writes its own logs to /var/log/inventory/*.log, and those entries do not appear in Cloud Logging. What should you do?
options: Add a file to /etc/google-fluentd/config.d that tails the logs, then restart google-fluentd
Set the VM metadata key google-logging-enabled to TRUE and then reboot the virtual machine
Add a files receiver for the path and a pipeline in /etc/google-cloud-ops-agent/config.yaml
Create a log-based metric whose filter matches the path /var/log/inventory on the VM
explanation: The Ops Agent reads its user configuration from /etc/google-cloud-ops-agent/config.yaml, where a files receiver with include_paths and a pipeline that uses it collect extra log files after an agent restart. The google-fluentd directory belongs to the legacy Logging agent, the metadata key does not add file paths, and a log-based metric cannot collect logs that were never ingested.
