serviceAccount:fin-prod.svc.id.goog[billing/payments-ksa]
serviceAccount:fin-prod.svc.id.goog[payments-ksa/billing]
explanation: The member format is serviceAccount:PROJECT_ID.svc.id.goog[NAMESPACE/KSA_NAME], so the project's workload pool is followed by the namespace and then the Kubernetes ServiceAccount name. The iam.gserviceaccount.com address would be an IAM service account, and the other two options reverse the namespace and account or use the namespace in place of the project ID.

question: Workload Identity Federation for GKE was just enabled on the Standard cluster prod in us-central1, but the existing node pool default-pool still exposes the Compute Engine metadata server to Pods. Which command fixes the node pool?
options: gcloud container clusters update prod --location=us-central1 --workload-pool=PROJECT_ID.svc.id.goog --enable-autoupgrade
gcloud container node-pools update default-pool --cluster=prod --location=us-central1 --workload-metadata=GKE_METADATA
gcloud container node-pools update default-pool --cluster=prod --location=us-central1 --service-account=PROJECT_ID.svc.id.goog
gcloud container node-pools update default-pool --cluster=prod --location=us-central1 --workload-metadata=GCE_METADATA
explanation: In Standard clusters, existing node pools must be updated with --workload-metadata=GKE_METADATA so that they run the GKE metadata server. GCE_METADATA is the setting that exposes the node's Compute Engine metadata server, the cluster-level workload pool is already set, and the workload pool is not a node service account.

question: Your team has created a new GKE Autopilot cluster and wants Pods to authenticate to Google Cloud APIs with Workload Identity Federation for GKE. What must be done at the cluster level first?
options: Recreate the cluster in Standard mode, because Autopilot clusters do not support the feature at all
Run gcloud container clusters update with --workload-pool=PROJECT_ID.svc.id.goog before configuring Pods
Nothing, because the feature is always enabled in Autopilot; configure the Kubernetes and IAM side directly
Create a node pool with --workload-metadata=GKE_METADATA and then migrate the Pods onto that pool
explanation: In Autopilot, Workload Identity Federation for GKE is always enabled, so you can go straight to configuring Kubernetes ServiceAccounts and IAM grants. The workload-pool and workload-metadata settings are Standard-cluster steps, and Autopilot node pools are managed by Google, so you do not create them yourself.

question: An SRE will spend the afternoon running many gcloud commands as ops-sa@ops-prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com and already holds Service Account Token Creator on it. They do not want to add a flag to every command. Which command should they run?
options: gcloud config set auth/impersonate_service_account ops-sa@ops-prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com
gcloud auth activate-service-account ops-sa@ops-prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com
gcloud config set core/account ops-sa@ops-prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com
gcloud config set core/impersonate_service_account ops-sa@ops-prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com
explanation: Setting the auth/impersonate_service_account property makes every gcloud command request short-lived credentials for that service account, and gcloud config unset reverses it. activate-service-account needs a key file, setting core/account to the service account does not provide credentials for it, and the property lives in the auth section, not core.

question: A developer is testing a Python application locally with the Cloud Client Libraries. The code must run as app-sa@dev-prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com, and the organization blocks service account keys. Which command should the developer run?
options: gcloud iam service-accounts keys create adc.json --iam-account=app-sa@dev-prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com
gcloud config set auth/impersonate_service_account app-sa@dev-prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com
gcloud auth application-default login --impersonate-service-account=app-sa@dev-prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com
gcloud auth login --cred-file=app-sa.json --impersonate-service-account=app-sa@dev-prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com
explanation: Client libraries read Application Default Credentials, and application-default login with the impersonation flag creates a local ADC file that uses short-lived credentials for app-sa. The auth/impersonate_service_account property only affects gcloud commands, and both key-based options are blocked by the organization and are not recommended.

question: Policy says your user account may only impersonate hop-sa, and only hop-sa may impersonate target-sa. You run gcloud config set auth/impersonate_service_account hop-sa@sec-prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com,target-sa@sec-prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com. According to the gcloud CLI documentation, which grants make this chain work?
options: Your user needs Token Creator on hop-sa, and hop-sa needs Token Creator on target-sa
target-sa needs Token Creator on hop-sa, and your user needs it on target-sa
Your user needs Token Creator on both hop-sa and target-sa, and hop-sa needs no roles
Your user needs Service Account User on hop-sa, and hop-sa needs it on target-sa
explanation: For a comma-separated delegation chain, the active account must hold roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator on the first service account, and each account must hold it on the next one in the list. Service Account User grants actAs, not token creation, and the other options either break the stated policy or reverse the direction of the chain.

question: You must call the private Cloud Run service https://inv-abc-uc.a.run.app with curl as invoker-sa@ops-prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com, which you are allowed to impersonate. You must not create a key or call the service with your own identity. How do you get the bearer token?
options: gcloud auth print-identity-token --impersonate-service-account=invoker-sa@ops-prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com --audiences=https://inv-abc-uc.a.run.app
gcloud auth print-identity-token --audiences=https://inv-abc-uc.a.run.app --include-email --token-format=full
gcloud config set core/account invoker-sa@ops-prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com, then run gcloud auth print-identity-token
gcloud iam service-accounts keys create inv.json --iam-account=invoker-sa@ops-prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com, then activate it
explanation: Cloud Run authenticates callers with Google-signed ID tokens, and print-identity-token with impersonation and the service URL as audience returns one for invoker-sa without a key. Without impersonation, the token represents your own account, a key is forbidden, and setting core/account to a service account does not give gcloud credentials for it.

question: A batch process uses generateIdToken in the IAM Service Account Credentials API to obtain ID tokens for report-sa and wants each token to last 6 hours. An administrator added report-sa to constraints/iam.allowServiceAccountCredentialLifetimeExtension, but the tokens still expire after 1 hour. What should you do?
options: Set the lifetime field of the generateIdToken request to 21600s now that the constraint applies
Accept the fixed 1-hour ID token lifetime and have the process request a fresh token before expiry
Enforce constraints/iam.serviceAccountKeyExpiryHours with 8h so that the issued tokens last longer
Grant roles/iam.serviceAccountOpenIdTokenCreator at the organization to unlock longer lifetimes
explanation: Google-signed OIDC ID tokens from generateIdToken are valid for 1 hour, while the lifetime-extension constraint raises the maximum lifetime of OAuth access tokens to 12 hours. The key expiry constraint applies only to user-managed keys, and granting a role at a higher level changes who can mint tokens, not how long they last.

question: You must give an external partner a link to download one object from a private bucket for 15 minutes. Your organization blocks service account keys. A service account report-sa can read the object. What should you do?
options: Grant allUsers roles/storage.objectViewer on the bucket for 15 minutes and then remove the binding again
Get Key Admin on report-sa, create a new JSON key and pass it to gcloud storage sign-url with --private-key-file
Get Service Account User on report-sa and run gcloud storage sign-url with --duration=15m and impersonation
Get Token Creator on report-sa and run gcloud storage sign-url with --duration=15m and impersonation of report-sa
explanation: gcloud storage sign-url can sign through an impersonated service account, which uses the signBlob permission in Token Creator, so no key is needed. Service Account User grants actAs, not signing, so that impersonation would fail. A public grant exposes the whole bucket, and creating a key is blocked and not recommended.

question: A team's deployment script creates a new key for deploy-sa on every release and never deletes old ones. Key creation has suddenly started failing, although the org policy permits keys in this project. What is the most likely cause?
options: The project reached its quota of 10 service accounts, which also caps the number of keys it can create
The key creation constraint is enforced automatically once a service account has created ten keys
User-managed keys expire after 90 days by default, and expired keys block the creation of new keys
A service account can have at most 10 keys, so the limit was reached; delete unused keys or go keyless
explanation: Google documents that a service account can have up to 10 keys, so a script that never deletes keys eventually fails. By default, user-managed keys never expire, the service account quota limits accounts rather than keys, and the key creation constraint is never turned on automatically by key count.

question: Your organization allows service account keys in one legacy project only. Security now requires every key created in that project to stop working 30 days after it is created. What should you do?
options: Set constraints/iam.serviceAccountKeyExpiryHours to allow 720h on that project so that new keys expire
Add the project's accounts to iam.allowServiceAccountCredentialLifetimeExtension with a 720h value
Create every key with gcloud iam service-accounts keys create --key-file-type=json --expiry=30d
Enforce iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation on that project with a 30-day condition on it
explanation: By default, keys never expire, and the iam.serviceAccountKeyExpiryHours constraint sets a validity period, such as 720h, for newly created keys. The key creation constraint blocks creation rather than setting a lifetime, the lifetime-extension constraint applies to short-lived access tokens, and keys create has no expiry flag.

question: An application on a partner's on-premises server must keep using a key for sync-sa until federation is supported. You are rotating the key. Which sequence follows Google's guidance and avoids an outage?
options: Delete the old key first so that it cannot be misused, then create a new key and switch the app to it
Disable sync-sa, create a new key while it is disabled, then re-enable sync-sa and switch the app
Create a new key, switch the app to it, disable the old key, confirm nothing breaks, then delete the old key
Create a new key, delete the old key immediately to save time, then update the app to use the new one
explanation: Google recommends disabling a key before deleting it, so you can re-enable it if something still depends on it, and the replacement must be in place first. Deleting the old key before the switch causes an outage, and disabling the whole account interrupts every workload that uses it.

question: During an incident you must immediately stop a suspected leaked key with ID 2f9c41ab for etl-sa@data-prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com, while keeping the option to restore it. Other keys and workloads of etl-sa must keep working, and the console does not offer a disable action for keys. Which command should you run?
options: gcloud iam service-accounts keys disable 2f9c41ab --iam-account=etl-sa@data-prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com
gcloud iam service-accounts keys delete 2f9c41ab --iam-account=etl-sa@data-prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com
gcloud iam service-accounts keys list --iam-account=etl-sa@data-prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com --managed-by=user
gcloud iam service-accounts disable etl-sa@data-prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com --project=data-prj
explanation: keys disable blocks one key and can be reversed with keys enable, and Google notes that disabling keys requires the gcloud CLI or REST API rather than the console. Disabling the whole account would stop every workload that uses etl-sa, deleting the key cannot be undone, and listing keys does not block anything.

question: Your organization was created in 2025. A vendor's on-premises appliance can authenticate only with a service account key file and supports no federation. Security has approved a single key for vendor-sa in the project vendor-int. What should you do?
options: Have an Org Policy Administrator override iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation on vendor-int only
Generate a key pair locally and upload the public key to vendor-sa, which the security baseline does not block
Stop enforcing iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation at the organization so that any project can create keys
Grant yourself roles/iam.serviceAccountKeyAdmin on vendor-sa, which lets you bypass the key creation constraint
explanation: When a key is truly unavoidable, the narrowest fix is a project-level exception to the key creation constraint, made by someone with roles/orgpolicy.policyAdmin. The constraint applies even to principals with key creation permission, removing it at the organization is far too broad, and the baseline also blocks key upload through iam.disableServiceAccountKeyUpload.

question: An application on Amazon EC2 in AWS account 111122223333 must call Google Cloud APIs without service account keys. You already created the workload identity pool aws-pool. Which command creates the provider?
options: gcloud iam workload-identity-pools create-cred-config projects/123/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/aws-pool --aws --output-file=aws.json
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers create-oidc aws-prov --location=global --workload-identity-pool=aws-pool --issuer-uri=https://sts.amazonaws.com
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers create-aws aws-prov --location=global --workload-identity-pool=aws-pool --account-id=111122223333
gcloud iam workforce-pools providers create-oidc aws-prov --location=global --workforce-pool=aws-pool --issuer-uri=https://sts.amazonaws.com
explanation: AWS workloads federate through a dedicated AWS provider type, created with providers create-aws and the 12-digit AWS account ID. An OIDC provider with an STS issuer is not how AWS federation is configured, workforce pools are for human users, and create-cred-config produces the client configuration file after the provider exists.

question: A workload on a Microsoft Azure VM uses a managed identity registered in Microsoft Entra ID and must call Google Cloud APIs without keys. Which provider should you add to the workload identity pool?
options: An OIDC provider with issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com/ and a tenant attribute condition
A SAML provider created in a workforce pool that uses the federation metadata of the Entra ID tenant
An AWS provider that is created with the Azure subscription ID supplied as the value of --account-id
An OIDC provider with issuer https://sts.windows.net/TENANT_ID and the app ID URI as the allowed audience
explanation: Azure workloads federate through an OIDC provider whose issuer is the Entra ID tenant, such as https://sts.windows.net/TENANT_ID, with the application ID URI as the allowed audience. Workforce pools are for people, the AWS provider type only accepts AWS accounts, and the GitHub issuer only accepts GitHub Actions tokens.

question: GitLab SaaS CI jobs from your GitLab group (group ID 7654321) must deploy to Google Cloud through Workload Identity Federation. GitLab SaaS uses one issuer URL for all customers. Which attribute condition should you set on the provider?
options: google.subject=assertion.sub
assertion.aud=='https://gitlab.com'
assertion.namespace_id=='7654321'
assertion.repository_owner=='7654321'
explanation: Because GitLab SaaS shares one issuer, Google requires an attribute condition that accepts only tokens from your group, and the documented condition checks the namespace_id claim. repository_owner is a GitHub Actions claim, an audience check does not tell groups apart, and google.subject=assertion.sub is an attribute mapping, not a condition.

question: A security reviewer objects to committing the Workload Identity Federation credential configuration file for a Jenkins pipeline to a private repository, arguing that it is equivalent to a service account key. What is the correct response?
options: It should be replaced with a key, because credential configuration files expire one hour after creation
It must be rotated every 90 days like a key, because it contains a private key used to sign token requests
It is not a secret, because it only names the token source, pool, provider and the account to impersonate
It must be kept in Secret Manager, because it embeds a long-lived refresh token for the service account
explanation: Google states that a credential configuration file defines where to get external credentials, which pool and provider to use and which service account to impersonate, and that it contains no private key and need not be kept confidential. It holds no refresh token and does not expire after an hour, and replacing it with a key would reintroduce a long-lived secret.

question: You receive two requests. First, employees must sign in to the Google Cloud console with their Okta identities without Cloud Identity accounts. Second, an on-premises Jenkins server must call Google Cloud APIs without keys. Which features should you use?
options: Workforce Identity Federation for the employees and Workload Identity Federation for Jenkins
Workload Identity Federation for the employees and Workforce Identity Federation for Jenkins
Workforce Identity Federation for both requests, using a separate provider for the Jenkins server
Workload Identity Federation for both requests, using separate pools for employees and Jenkins
explanation: Workforce Identity Federation lets human users from an external IdP access Google Cloud, while Workload Identity Federation lets non-human workloads such as CI servers exchange external credentials for Google Cloud access. Swapping or merging the two misuses each feature's intended principal type.

question: A service account was deleted by mistake 12 days ago. The DeleteServiceAccount audit log entry shows its unique ID, 108811234567890123456. Which command restores it?
options: gcloud iam service-accounts create old-sa --display-name="restored"
gcloud beta iam service-accounts undelete 108811234567890123456
gcloud iam service-accounts enable old-sa@prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com
gcloud iam service-accounts undelete old-sa@prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com
explanation: Undelete is a beta gcloud command that requires the deleted account's numeric unique ID and works for up to 30 days after deletion. It is not available in the GA command group and does not accept an email address, enable only applies to disabled accounts, and creating a new account with the same name produces a different identity with no roles.

question: ingest-sa was deleted 10 days ago. Yesterday a colleague created a new service account that is also named ingest-sa. Your attempt to undelete the original account now fails. What should you do?
options: Grant the original roles to the new account, because undelete only works within 7 days of deletion
Delete the new ingest-sa, then undelete the original by its unique ID so that it keeps its own roles
Disable the new ingest-sa, because a disabled account with the same name does not block an undelete
Do nothing more, because the new ingest-sa automatically inherits every role of the original account
explanation: Undelete fails while a new account with the same name exists, so you must delete the new one first, and the restored account keeps its original identity and roles. A new account with the same name is a separate identity that inherits nothing, undelete works for up to 30 days, and a disabled account still exists.

question: You believe that the service account old-batch-sa is no longer used, but you are not certain, and production outages are costly. What is the safest way to retire it?
options: Delete all of its keys, because without keys no workload can authenticate as that service account
Delete it right away, because a recreated account with the same name automatically regains its roles
Remove it from every allow policy and then delete it, because role removals are easy to reverse
Disable it first, watch for failures for a while, and delete it only once nothing has broken
explanation: Google recommends disabling unused service accounts before deleting them, because a disabled account can be re-enabled immediately if something breaks. A recreated account is a new identity without the old roles, attached workloads authenticate without keys, and reconstructing removed role bindings is error-prone.

question: Before a cleanup, you want a list of when each service account in the project data-prj last authenticated to a Google API. Which command provides this?
options: gcloud iam service-accounts list --project=data-prj --filter=disabled:false --format="table(email,disabled)"
gcloud policy-intelligence query-activity --activity-type=serviceAccountLastAuthentication --project=data-prj
gcloud asset search-all-iam-policies --scope=projects/data-prj --query="memberTypes:serviceAccount"
gcloud policy-intelligence query-activity --activity-type=serviceAccountKeyLastAuthentication --project=data-prj
explanation: Activity Analyzer's query-activity command with the serviceAccountLastAuthentication activity type lists the most recent authentication time for each service account. The serviceAccountKeyLastAuthentication type reports per key instead, listing service accounts shows no usage data, and searching IAM policies shows grants, not activity.

question: Service account insights flag gws-sync-sa as unused for 90 days. This account uses domain-wide delegation to call Google Workspace APIs every night. What should you do before you disable or delete it?
options: Check Activity Analyzer instead, because it does record authentications made with domain-wide delegation
Check whether it has keys, because an account without user-managed keys cannot be in use at all
Delete it right away, because insights record authentications to every Google API, Workspace included
Check Cloud Monitoring usage metrics, because insights do not track domain-wide delegation calls
explanation: Google notes that authentications to Google APIs outside Google Cloud, such as domain-wide delegation to Workspace APIs, are not tracked by Activity Analyzer or service account insights, and recommends cross-checking with Cloud Monitoring service account usage metrics. Keyless accounts can still be used through attachment or impersonation.

question: A Cloud Scheduler job must call a private Cloud Run service every hour as sched-sa@ops-prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com. Which configuration follows least privilege?
options: Grant sched-sa roles/run.invoker on the service and set the job's OIDC service account and audience to the service
Grant sched-sa roles/cloudscheduler.admin on the project and create the job with an OAuth service account and scope
Grant allUsers roles/run.invoker on the service so that Cloud Scheduler can reach it without any token
Grant the Cloud Scheduler service agent roles/run.admin on the project and omit all authentication flags
explanation: Cloud Scheduler can attach an OIDC ID token for sched-sa with --oidc-service-account-email and --oidc-token-audience, and the Cloud Run Invoker role on that one service authorizes the call. Scheduler Admin does not authorize invoking Cloud Run, making the service public removes its protection, and Run Admin on the project is far broader than needed.

question: Service accounts are kept in a central project named sa-hub. A developer with roles/iam.serviceAccountUser on app-sa in sa-hub tries to create a VM in another project that runs as app-sa, and the request fails with an error naming an organization policy constraint. What is the likely cause?
options: iam.disableCrossProjectServiceAccountUsage is enforced on sa-hub and must be relaxed there for this use
iam.automaticIamGrantsForDefaultServiceAccounts blocks attaching any service account from other projects
iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation stops app-sa from issuing the credentials that the VM needs
The developer also needs roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator on app-sa before they can attach the account
explanation: The iam.disableCrossProjectServiceAccountUsage constraint prevents service accounts in a project from being attached to resources in other projects, so it must not be enforced on the project that owns app-sa. Token Creator is not required to attach an account, the default service account constraint only controls automatic Editor grants, and attached VMs do not use keys.

question: A central identity team wants to stop developers from creating service accounts in any project under the Apps folder, without removing the developers' other permissions in those projects. What should you do?
options: Enforce the iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation constraint on the Apps folder
Enforce the iam.automaticIamGrantsForDefaultServiceAccounts constraint on the Apps folder
Enforce the iam.managed.disableServiceAccountCreation constraint on the Apps folder
Remove roles/iam.serviceAccountUser from every developer in the projects under the folder
explanation: The iam.managed.disableServiceAccountCreation constraint blocks creating new service accounts while leaving the rest of the developers' permissions unchanged. The key creation constraint blocks keys, not accounts, the default service account constraint only affects automatic Editor grants, and Service Account User controls actAs, not creation.
